#6249. The notion of ‘positive masculinity’ is dividing the male studies field

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Researchers’ debate shapes how mental health experts advise men

Does “positive masculinity” exist or reinforce sexist gender norms? Researchers grappling with that question say the answer will help determine how doctors and therapists treat men.

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

Ryon McDermott set out seven years ago to create a new scale measuring masculinity. McDermott, along with other researchers studying male psyches, was tired of the field’s long-standing assertion that the manlier the man, the worse his outcomes. It was high time to measure masculinity in a positive light.

For almost half a century, the many social science scales that measure gender or masculinity have consistently shown that rigid fealty to Western masculine norms — such as prioritizing work, power-seeking and status — link with poor mental and physical health. Endorsement of such norms also correlates with misogynistic beliefs and violent behaviors, including sexual violence, studies have shown.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

But giving men a talking-to about their many defects rarely lands well. Nor does that negative focus help men thrive. But what approach would help? “We don’t really have a definition of men’s health. If we don’t know what we are going towards, how can we even do this [research]?” says Matt Englar-Carlson, a counseling expert at California State University, Fullerton.

What traits, the researchers wondered, define a healthy man? And could a healthy reframing of manhood improve men’s outcomes, such as by getting them to the doctor or lowering their high rates of social isolation, depression and even death by suicide?

Those questions would cleave the field, though as fights go, this one has been downright nice. McDermott, a psychologist of masculinity at the University of South Alabama in Mobile, would ultimately question positive masculinity’s very existence. Meanwhile, his friends and collaborators at Movember — a nonprofit research organization based in Richmond, Australia that encourages mustache-growing in November to spark conversations around men’s health issues — are poised for a 2027 launch of the Healthy Manhood Index. That scale uses a positive framing and is designed to gauge men’s strengths, while illuminating areas for improvement.

The first gender measurement scale emerged almost a century ago. It positioned femininity and masculinity at opposite poles, with researchers assuming that the most gender-conforming men and women were the healthiest.

That thinking has since unraveled. As women began smashing gender barriers, by doing everything from donning pants to entering the workforce, penalties for women acting more masculine largely disappeared.

Inspired by the feminist movement, researchers began studying the masculine psyche. Yet they largely framed masculinity as a barrier to health. The Male Role Norms Inventory, one of the most popular masculinity scales in use today, exemplifies that focus. Individuals rank statements like: “A man must stand on his own two feet and never depend on other people to help him do things.”

The higher the score on that and more than 60 similar statements appearing in popular masculinity scales used over the past 50 or so years, the worse men’s outcomes, McDermott and his colleagues at Movember reported in July in Men and Masculinities. “Manlier” men often struggle with depression and substance use and engage in sexual aggression. They also tend to avoid asking for help or taking precautionary health measures, such as wearing a mask during the COVID-19 pandemic.

But almost 80 percent of the statements used frame masculinity as a problem to be solved, the team found. That deficit lens biases the findings, argues coauthor and social psychologist Peter Fisher of the Movember Institute of Men’s Health, the organization’s research arm. “If the only tools you have available to you are looking for deficits, you will find deficits,” says Fisher, who is based in Santa Monica, Calif.

That negative framing has also seeped into public discourse, so much so that some people now intuitively link “masculinity” with the word “toxic.”

Yet those most macho of men are the outliers, the small percentage who score highest on masculinity scales, Englar-Carlson says. He suspects that what really matters for health is flexibility around when to behave in certain ways. Stoicism, a typically masculine-coded trait, can be calming in emergencies but scary when a man experiences a mental health crisis and refuses help.

Englar-Carlson and psychologist Mark Kiselica, of Penn State University, Harrisburg, developed the Positive Psychology Positive Masculinity, or PPPM, paradigm in 2010. Public health experts, therapists and others should focus on men’s strengths not deficits, they argued.

The ideas in PPPM are what McDermott began trying to turn into a masculinity scale a few years later. But his efforts sent him into a tailspin.

He and his colleagues began by identifying positive traits that people linked more with men than women. The team generated a list of 79 possible positive male attributes based on findings from focus groups and studies of positive masculinity and positive psychology, such as “having a good sense of humor,” “serving country or community” and “having passion for one’s work.” More than 1,000 individuals then rated those attributes on a scale from 1 for “strongly disagree” to 7 for “strongly agree” along three dimensions: positive, typically expected of men and typically expected of women.

Roughly 40 percent of the attributes, particularly those pertaining to protective behaviors and assertiveness, were seen as both positive and expected more of men than of women, McDermott and his colleagues reported in 2019 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

But the study also showed that both men and women scored above the midpoint on almost all the allegedly male attributes. That could mean the supposedly gendered attributes had little to do with gender. And for many measures, such as patience and having good hygiene, women scored higher than men. Could that mean that the study’s list was rebranding attributes from feminism as masculine? The idea didn’t sit well with McDermott.

Then, the team’s research took a dark turn. The researchers had respondents fill out both their new masculinity survey and a scale measuring sexist beliefs. That revealed that the more strongly respondents endorsed masculine ideals, the more likely they were to endorse sexist beliefs, the team’s unpublished work shows. Think about a statement like, “A good man should be strong,” McDermott says. For many people, that translates to “a good woman should be weak.”

“I’ve looked at this across three different samples [of people], and I find the same results each time,” McDermott says. “Whenever you define masculinity, you are inherently defining it against femininity.”

Most attributes are neither male nor female, but human, McDermott has come to believe. And gendering those universal traits merely reinforces sexist stereotypes. The work has left him gutted. “I really thought that there was such thing as positive masculinity,” he says. “But now I believe that it can never truly be positive.”

Fisher is well aware of McDermott’s journey. “He’s been trying to create a positive masculinity scale, or isolate the positive characteristics of masculinity, for a while,” Fisher says. “And he’s been struggling.”

Perhaps McDermott has set too high a bar, Fisher says. Rather than trying to identify and measure masculinity through beliefs, he says, why not focus on men’s actions?

So for the past several years, Fisher and colleagues have been doing just that. They have organized numerous focus groups and tested survey statements with some 12,000 individuals across six countries. Besides addressing the lack of age and cultural diversity used to create most masculinity scales currently in use, Fisher and his team hope that their scale will provide men with a blueprint for what constitutes healthy behavior.

Below are qualities Movember Institute of Men’s Health researchers are evaluating to develop a new masculinity scale. The items are preliminary and may not appear in the final version. The rows show counterproductive behaviors that result from pressures facing men, healthy responses and possible wording for survey statements the men would then rate.

All the statements in the Healthy Manhood Index start with “I” plus a verb, such as “I do,” “I talk” or “I check in,” Fisher says. For instance, men often feel pressure to restrict their emotions, so the healthy response would be for men to open up emotionally. The index might have men rate a statement like: “I share difficult things I’m going through with people I trust.” Crucially, the higher the score on the index, the healthier the man.

Fisher’s goal is to move men toward healthy behaviors without alienating them. “We just want to meet men where they are,” he says.

A debate that could easily become acrimonious has remained almost cloyingly friendly. McDermott refers to Fisher as “brilliant.” Fisher credits McDermott for “letting the data change his mind.”

Researchers in the field recognize that they share the same goals, says psychological researcher Michael Addis of Clark University in Worcester, Mass. They want men to be healthier and to treat others, including women and seemingly less masculine men, with respect. “The question is how do we do that? We either sell them on a new masculinity, or we say ‘…. masculinity is always going to be in some ways a box,’” he says.

Though discussions around how to frame masculinity can feel wonky, the stakes are real, Addis and psychiatrist and behavioral scientist Ethan Hoffmann of Stanford University wrote in 2024 in Psychology of Men & Masculinities.

Consider suicide. Men who strongly endorsed masculine norms were less likely than others to seek help for depression and more likely to die by suicide, researchers reported in 2025 in Psychiatry International.

Theoretically, public health campaigns aimed at men can help. But what form should they take? A positive masculinity campaign may recast a statement like, “real men never ask for help” to “real men know when it’s time to ask for help,” Addis and Hoffman write. But a campaign that rejects gender labels may roll out statements like: “Real men aren’t real: It’s a fiction that could cost you your life.”

Such postgender messaging may feel too abstract for the average guy, Fisher says. Convincing a 65-year-old man to stay on top of his prostate cancer appointments is hard enough without trying to shift his worldview.

McDermott counters that positive masculinity “makes the sex role stuff continue,” enshrining the idea that gender roles and hierarchies constitute a necessary organizing principle for societies.

Reconciliation may be possible, Addis says. Policy makers and public health experts could first rope men in with a more positive masculine approach. Then over time, they could help men question and relinquish gender norms. “I call it dancing with the devil,” or temporarily adopting the gendered approach as a means to a desired end, he says.

However the debate unfurls, researchers are writing their own script on how to fight like real men — or real people. “There’s a lot of men in the psychology of men [field] who have worked really hard to not let our egos get in the way of good work,” Addis says. “It’s sort of like practice what you preach.”

If you or someone you care about may be at risk of suicide, the 988 Suicide and Crisis Lifeline offers free, 24/7 support, information and local resources from trained counselors. Call or text 988 or chat at 988lifeline.org.

C.M. Galvez-Sánchez et al. Exploring the role of masculinity in male suicide: A systematic review. Psychiatry International. 2025. doi: 10.3390/psychiatryint6010002

E. Hoffman and E.M. Addis. To reconstruct or deconstruct? A fundamental question for men and masculinities. Psychology of Men & Masculinities. 2024. doi: 10.1037/men0000440

#6248. The Age of the Computer Virus Is Over. Welcome to the Era of the AI Autoimmune Disease.

The cure for our cybersecurity crisis might actually be what’s causing this havoc in the first place.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

There’s a quote often falsely attributed to Vladimir Lenin that “There are decades where nothing happens; and there are weeks where decades happen.” The cybersecurity world experienced one of those weeks earlier this month, and the ramifications have sent shockwaves through the halls of government and the average American home.

Was this an anomaly, or the first sign of an anarchic AI-fueled collapse?

People were already grumbling that the AI bubble was about to burst when the story of then-Nvidia CEO Jensen Huang’s alleged indiscretions broke. Then, on November 12, Microsoft suffered a massive outage, hobbling an email service countless companies rely on. The next day, just as people’s inboxes were finally refilling, the FAA began grounding airplanes nationwide due to some unspecified computer error.

The demon in the machine evidently took the weekend off but came back with a vengeance on Monday. That’s when major disruptions hit banks like Chase, Wells Fargo, and Bank of America. America had been hit in its workplace, its skies, and even its pocketbook, but the final blow (for now) struck at a spot most Americans will never even see. On November 17, reports emerged that a significant outage had struck the NSA’s own internal, heavily classified network.

After that, the conversation shifted. People were no longer wondering whether the AI bubble would burst; they were asking whether AI would take us down with it.

In the aftermath, Congress decided there was no choice but to act. It was time to finally take a stand on AI that would prevent these kinds of outages in the future, even if nobody was terribly clear on just what had caused these disruptions, or what exactly AI had to do with them. There were bipartisan calls to assemble the “Superintelligence Task Force” to combat cyberattacks, and a series of amendments was proposed for the National Defense Authorization Act to limit China’s access to American chip-making tools, curbing its ability to produce malicious AI.

But what if we’re thinking about this all wrong? What if AI wasn’t attacking us at all? Maybe the AI was just doing its job, trying to strengthen our defenses, and its well-intentioned efforts had devastating consequences.

“Nobody ever asked: What if, in the name of progress, we were creating the ripest attack surface in human history?” Nicole Perlroth, a cybersecurity journalist and author of the book This Is How They Tell Me the World Ends: The Cyberweapons Arms Race, wrote in a thread on X. “We are entering a period of unprecedented technological instability.”

Perlroth argued that the official story being put forward by the affected institutions, that the outages were due to update issues rather than overt cyberattacks, isn’t a lie, and that’s precisely the problem.

What Perlroth posited in her thread, later supported by reporting in The Washington Sun, was that the AI these organizations had integrated into their systems had become efficient at finding critical vulnerabilities. Too efficient, actually. AI, it seems, had found “3X the number of vulnerabilities discovered in the same period last year.” On the surface, that might seem like a good thing. But it’s not enough to simply identify a weak spot—you also have to fix it before anybody else finds it.

“Mean time to exploit those vulnerabilities has collapsed to NEGATIVE SEVEN DAYS,” Perlroth wrote. “AI allows attackers to find/exploit vulns far faster than software makers have time to fix them.” Offensive AI tools like ARTEX can play a role in that exploitation, Perlroth acknowledged, but what’s likely playing a bigger role in these system outages isn’t an outside invader, but rather the system unintentionally damaging itself in a misguided attempt to patch the weak spots.

The rapid AI-powered discovery of these vulnerabilities “creates enormous pressure to compress patching windows and accelerate software updates,” Perlroth noted, “increasing the likelihood these fixes break things in unexpected, cascading ways.” In effect, the Silicon Valley adage of “move fast and break things” steamrolled the the principle of “first, do no harm,” long associated with the Hippocratic Oath.

Perhaps that ancient oath of physicians should make a comeback as we move into this new age of technology. After all, we’ve used medical terms for technological matters before; even the most “seasoned” senators and congresspeople on Capitol Hill have heard of a computer “virus.” That’s likely the framework lawmakers are using as they try to legislate the genie back into the bottle.

But a virus is a foreign agent, an outside entity that creeps into the body and wreaks havoc. What appears to be happening with the AI-associated outages we just experienced is more akin to a different medical concern: an autoimmune disease. In those instances, it is the body’s own immune system that, in a misguided effort to protect itself, mistakes healthy cells for harmful foreign agents and winds up damaging the body it’s intended to defend.

In the rush to repair these AI-identified vulnerabilities, The Washington Sun summarized, the organizations are “trying to push through a lot of patches all at once—more than the system was designed for,” and in doing so, are introducing entirely new flaws and bugs.

Knowing exactly what you’re dealing with can make all the difference when you’re trying to fix a problem, whether it’s in the human body or in a computer system. A misdiagnosis on either front can have catastrophic consequences.

Let’s hope our lawmakers and engineers have brushed up on their digital pathology.

Michale Natale is a News Editor for the Hearst Enthusiast Group. As a writer and researcher, he has produced written and audio-visual content for more than fifteen years, spanning historical periods from the dawn of early man to the Golden Age of Hollywood. His stories for the Enthusiast Group have involved coordinating with organizations like the National Parks Service and the Secret Service, and travelling to notable historical sites and archaeological digs, from excavations of America’ earliest colonies to the former homes of Edgar Allan Poe.

All the must-see supermoons, meteor showers, star clusters, constellations and deep sky objects this winter — and the gear you need to see them.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Winter is an incredible time for stargazing. With the long hours of darkness and an impressive variety of celestial objects on display, it's easy to fall in love with the night sky during the winter. Whether you have binoculars, a telescope, a smart telescope or are just observing with your eyes, there's something for everyone to enjoy over the coming months.

We've listed all the best sights to see this winter, including the supermoons, star clusters, galaxies and deep-sky nebulae that are best placed in the sky in December, January and February. We see the return of Orion and the Pleiades, with Jupiter and Saturn also making their way back into the night sky, while December also has one of the best and brightest meteor showers of the entire year — the Geminids.

This is by no means an exhaustive list of everything you can see — we'd be here until July — but just a collection of some of our favorite winter sights. Some, like the supermoons and planets, are specific to 2026/2027 timings, but the constellations and deep sky objects we see over the winter are something stargazers look forward to all year. Something to get us through the cold, dreary weather, and a reassuring sign that we made it through another year.

A composite photo of a full supermoon rising into the sky.

This winter is host to three consecutive supermoons (in addition to the full Beaver Supermoon on Nov. 24, making four in a row). The first, and the most festive, is the Christmas Eve supermoon, peaking on December 24, 2026, at 01:28 UTC (which works out as late evening on the 23rd in North America). This last moon of the year is traditionally called the Cold Moon, and this supermoon will look up to 14% larger and 30% brighter than a normal full moon.

The first full moon of 2027, known as the Wolf Moon, peaks on January 22, 2027 at 12:17 UTC. Finally, the super Snow Moon peaks on February 20, 2027 at 23:24 UTC, coinciding with a penumbral lunar eclipse. This is when the sun, moon and Earth line up loosely during a full moon, causing the moon to pass through the Earth's faint outer shadow — the penumbra. During this type of eclipse, the moon only dims slightly, so it won't be nearly as dramatic as a blood moon eclipse.

A photo of an annular, or "ring of fire", solar eclipse.

Observers in South America and Africa will witness an annular solar eclipse on February 6, 2027, peaking at around 16:00 UTC. It will appear as a "ring of fire" in the sky, as an annular solar eclipse happens when the moon passes between Earth and the sun when the moon is near or at its farthest from Earth, known as apogee. Unlike a total solar eclipse, the sun isn't totally blocked, and the sky doesn't turn dark.

A photo of a bright planet glowing in the evening sky.

Since Saturn made its return to the evening sky in the fall, it rises earlier and earlier over the winter months, making this a great time to observe Saturn at a reasonable hour. There are still a few years before we will see the rings at full tilt again, but in 2026/2027 we can start to see more details in the rings after the planet appeared edge-on last year.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

To get a good glimpse of Saturn this winter, you'll need a telescope with at least 4 or 5 inches of aperture and a good eyepiece that gives you at least 100x magnification. Smart telescopes and binoculars don't have the reach, so this is a job for an observational telescope. But that's all right; the hill we'll die on is that there's nothing that'll take your breath away quite like seeing Saturn's rings with your own eyes.

Jupiter will reach opposition on the night of February 10-11, 2027, when it will be at its brightest and closest to Earth, making it appear its largest in the sky. This is the perfect time to observe it with your telescope to see the bands and the Great Red Spot, as well as its four Galilean moons. You'll be able to see the moons with a pair of big astronomy binoculars (we can see them with our 15x70’s), but you'll need a telescope to make out any of the finer details on the planet itself.

After almost a year of absence, Mars made its return to the evening sky in November (albeit quite late in the evening) and will reach opposition on February 19, 2027. Despite being one of our closest neighboring planets, Mars is notoriously difficult to get any meaningful observations with via a telescope, so its opposition is the best chance you'll have.

You'd be forgiven for thinking that because Mars is technically closer to Earth than Jupiter, Saturn and deep-sky objects like the Andromeda Galaxy or the Orion Nebula, viewing it through a telescope would be a breeze, but that's not the case. Mars is very small, with low-contrast features, and only comes observably close to Earth for a few months at a time around every 26-27 months, so it demands quite a lot from a telescope. Even with larger telescopes, it'll only show up as a fuzzy orange dot most of the time.

If you want to try viewing Mars with a telescope this opposition, you'll need 4-6 inches of aperture minimum, depending on what kind of telescope you have. However, for Mars, it's arguably more important to have good seeing (unfortunate with the nearly full moon on this day), excellent quality optics, a stable (preferably motorized) mount, a good focuser and an eyepiece with good eye relief that gives 100x magnification or more to observe any of the planet's finer details.

Alternatively, if you're more of a beginner and are just starting your stargazing hobby, you can head outside with just your eyes and go "Hey look, there's Mars. Cool!" and be done with it.

The Geminids meteor shower is active from December 4-20, peaking on the night of December 13-14, 2026. The waxing crescent moon sets early, leaving dark skies after around 9 pm for prime meteor viewing, and this is one of the few meteor showers that very kindly peaks before midnight.

The Geminids are one of the strongest meteor showers of the year, and this year’s show is expected to have around 120 to 150 meteors per hour under clear, dark skies — making it an exciting opportunity for astrophotography.

Unlike most meteor showers, which come from icy comets, the Geminids originate from a rocky asteroid called 3200 Phaethon. The debris from this asteroid is much denser than the dust from comets, making it able to survive deeper into the atmosphere before burning up. This results in brighter, stronger and more colorful fireballs than the other meteor showers.

If the Geminids left you hooked on meteor showers, you'll only have a few weeks to wait until the Ursids peak on December 22-23, 2026.

However, there are a couple of hurdles here. First, the activity rate is usually quite low — between 5 and 10 meteors per hour. Second, the nearly full moon will hinder visibility and limit sightings to only the brightest meteors. However, as they originate from Ursa Minor, which is circumpolar, the peak viewing time of 21:00-22:00 UTC is much friendlier than the showers that peak in the middle of the night, so it won't require an unreasonable amount of commitment if you do want to catch them.

The first meteor shower of 2027, the Quadrantids, is active between December 28, 2026 and January 28, 2027, peaking on the night of January 3-4, 2027. The thin waning crescent moon won't interfere with viewing conditions, and we could see up to 100-120 meteors per hour. The best time to view will be from midnight through to the pre-dawn hours, when the radiant point, Bootes, is highest in the sky.

Canis Major (the "Greater Dog") is visible over the winter months through until spring, and is easily recognisable by Sirius, the brightest star in the night sky. It's one of the closest stars to our solar system, sitting 8.6 light-years away, and due to its distance and apparent magnitude, its twinkling and flashes of color are particularly noticeable. This is known as scintillation, where turbulence in Earth's atmosphere bends starlight as it passes through different layers of air. It's especially noticeable when Sirius is low in the sky, as the light has more atmosphere to pass through.

You don't need any specialist gear to spot Sirius — it's easily visible with the naked eye. However, if you do have a pair of binoculars, you can even try to spot it in the daytime at certain times of the year.

Look above Canis Major, and you'll find Canis Minor — the "Little Dog". It primarily consists of two bright stars: Procyon and Gomeisa, the former making up a key part of the Winter Triangle and Winter Hexagon. Canis Minor is a fairly faint constellation, but a pair of binoculars will give you a better view.

Canis Minor and Canis Major are most famously known as the loyal hunting dogs of Orion, who spent seven years pursuing the Pleiades sisters to no avail. He should have just led with the fact that he had two dogs.

Speaking of Orion, one of the most recognizable sights in the night sky is Orion's belt, consisting of three bright stars in a straight line: Alnitak, Alnilam and Mintaka. Because of its prominence in the winter sky, Orion's belt has served as a universal celestial marker for navigation, timekeeping and mythologies across human history. The entire Orion constellation is a favorite among stargazers because there's so much to see, both with the naked eye and through binoculars or a telescope.

Another prominent feature of the Orion constellation is Betelgeuse. This red supergiant is easily visible to the naked eye, and astronomers expect it to explode as a supernova within the next 100,000 years. When that eventually happens, it will become visible in broad daylight and shine as brightly as the full moon for a few months. Betelgeuse, Sirius (Canis Major) and Procyon (Canis Minor) make up the Winter Triangle.

There's also Rigel, the brightest star in the constellation, which marks the hunter's foot, and Orion's Sword, a hanging line of stars just below the belt, which contains the Orion Nebula (more on that later).

Although Taurus returned to the evening sky in the fall, winter offers the best viewing time because it sits higher earlier in the evening. The brightest star in the constellation, Aldebaran, is easily recognizable as an orange-red star that marks the bull's eye.

With a pair of binoculars, you'll be able to see two beautiful star clusters — the Pleiades (M45) and the Hyades. The former is a bright open star cluster consisting of seven stars (also known as the Seven Sisters) that you can just about see with the naked eye under very dark skies, and the latter is a V-shaped open cluster that forms the face and head of the bull.

The Pleiades is an ideal first target if you're thinking of buying an entry-level smart telescope, and it's also easy to pick out in wide-field iPhone photos of the night sky.

Auriga is a pentagon-shaped constellation high in the sky between Taurus and Gemini, and is home to a few star clusters to observe this winter.

M36, the Pinwheel Cluster, contains around 60 to 100 stars and is located north of the star El Nath in Auriga. M38, known as the Starfish Cluster, contains over 100 stars, with its brightest forming an X shape, giving it a starfish-like appearance. Finally, M37, known as the Salt and Pepper Cluster, is the brightest and richest cluster in the constellation and contains over 500 stars.

Not only is Gemini the radiant point of the Geminids meteor shower, but its two most prominent stars, Pollux and Castor, are a very recognizable winter target in the night sky. Pollux is an orange giant star and the constellation's brightest point, while Castor appears blue. Although Castor looks like one star to the naked eye, it's actually a complex multiple star system, consisting of three distinct binary pairs: Castor A, Castor B and Castor C. With a small telescope, you can split Castor into its two main pairs, Castor Aa and Castor Ba.

Gemini also contains M35, a large open cluster also known as the Shoe Buckle Cluster, which you can easily view with binoculars.

It’s not an official constellation, but the Winter Hexagon (also known as the Winter Circle) is a recognizable pattern of prominent stars in the winter sky. It consists of Rigel (Orion), Aldebaran (Taurus), Capella (Auriga), Pollux (Gemini), Procyon (Canis Minor) and Sirius (Canis Major).

Once you spot all of the stars that make up the Winter Hexagon, it provides an easy way to navigate your way around the night sky with your binoculars or telescope.

Probably everyone's favorite nebula, largely because it's very easy to spot. It's located in Orion's sword, just below Orion's belt, and when conditions are dark enough, you can even see it with the naked eye and identify it in smartphone photos. Binoculars reveal it as a faint smudge, while telescopes give you a better view of the bright, glowing gas. It's also a wonderful target for smart telescopes with a wide field of view.

While you're there, you can find the Running Man Nebula, a bright reflection nebula complex located just north of the Orion Nebula — and it can be captured in the same frame if you're photographing it. If nebulas are your thing, Orion is absolutely packed with them, including the Casper the Friendly Ghost Nebula (M78), the Monkey Head Nebula (NGC 2174) and the Witch Head Nebula (IC 2118), although many of Orion's nebulas are quite faint and tricky to capture, requiring long integration times.

A photo of the Horsehead and Flame Nebulas

The Horsehead and Flame Nebula in Orion is another popular target for smart telescopes, as it takes up a big portion of the frame and doesn't need a super-long integration time to get a decent, web-ready image (although we'd always recommend shooting for as long as you can).

The Flame and Horsehead are technically two separate entities, but are often paired together due to their close apparent proximity, often fitting inside the same frame. The Flame Nebula is a bright, vibrant emission nebula that gets its name from its fiery network of dark, dense dust lanes. The Horsehead Nebula, on the other hand, is a dark nebula. It's composed of a dense cloud of molecular dust and gas that blocks the light from the emission nebula and stars around it. As the name suggests, this dark nebula takes on the form of a horse's head and neck.

The Rosette Nebula is a vast, star-forming region in the constellation of Monoceros and is a fantastic astrophotography target. Its large, flower-like appearance comes from stellar winds and radiation from the central cluster of young stars. The best time to view and photograph the Rosette Nebula is from January, when Monoceros climbs higher and higher in the evening sky.

The California Nebula lives in the constellation Perseus and gets its name from its resemblance to the U.S. state. This famous emission nebula is made up of ionized gas from the nearby Xi Persei, giving it its vibrant red and pink appearance. It has an apparent size of approximately 2.5 degrees, making it a great target for astrophotography and smart telescopes, as it appears quite large in the frame. Peak visibility of the California Nebula is from now until February.

12,000 light-years away, in the constellation Auriga, you'll find the Tadpole Nebula — a beautiful emission nebula and active stellar nursery. It spans 100 light-years across and makes for a stunning smart telescope target. It gets its name from the distinct, prominent gas and dust pillars that resemble cosmic tadpoles swimming through space — only these tadpoles are around 10 light-years long.

If you're using a smart telescope or astrophotography camera, you'll typically need an integration time of 2-3 hours to bring out more structure in the nebulosity, although longer sessions will yield better results.

Also in Auriga is the Flaming Star Nebula, although this nebula is much closer to Earth — around 1,500 light-years away — and spans about 5 light-years across. Despite being "smaller" than other targets, it appears quite big in the frame of a smart telescope due to its distance from Earth. It's best seen throughout late autumn and winter when Auriga is climbing high in the sky.

The Flaming Star Nebula is an emission and reflection nebula, with each type of nebulosity responding to different filters. In this instance, capturing two sets of data to stack in astrophotography software can help reveal more detail and colors. Broadband filter exposures capture the full range of visible light, including the blue light reflected by dust, as well as natural star colors. Narrowband or dual-band filters isolate specific emission wavelengths, such as hydrogen-alpha (Ha) and oxygen-III (OIII). By using these filters for separate sessions, your final image will show the red glow from the emission nebula and the blue tones from the reflective dust.

Kimberley Lane, E-commerce writer for Live Science, has tested a wide range of optical equipment, reviewing camera gear from Sony, Canon, OM System and more. With over 6 years of photography experience, her skills span across landscape and seascape photography, wildlife, astrophotography and portrait work. Her photos have been featured in a number of national magazines, including Digital Camera World and Cosmopolitan. She has also contributed to our sister site Space.com and Tech Radar, and she regularly uses binoculars and telescopes to stargaze in the dark skies of South Wales.

At a cliff site in Texas, archaeologists discovered hundreds of bison bones, stone tools and arrowheads, suggesting Indigenous people used "bison jumps" to hunt.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeologists have uncovered an extremely rare example of a "bison jump" in the Texas Panhandle, where a natural geological formation allowed Indigenous people to hunt North America's largest living land mammal for 3,000 years. The discovery confirms that the prehistoric hunting technique ‪—‬ which involved channeling a herd of bison into a stampede off a cliff, akin to "walking the plank" ‪—‬ was not limited to the northern Plains like experts previously thought.

"Bison jumping is an iconic, uniquely North American hunting technique that yielded some of the most productive food-getting events in the history of human hunting," researchers wrote in a study published online Nov. 9 in the journal American Antiquity.

Although jump sites are well known throughout the northern Plains, only one such site had ever been found in the southern Plains. But a second bison jump called Nighthawk has now been identified in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle, and researchers found that Indigenous people used the Nighthawk bison jump for millennia.

"Returning to the same place over and over again over 3,000 years shows that people had a significant connection to the Nighthawk hunting facility," study first author Gus Costa, an archaeologist at Rice University in Houston, said in a statement.

Nighthawk was found when bison remains began eroding from a bone bed (a place where bones naturally accumulate) underneath a roughly 65-foot-tall (20 meters) cliff spur. Archaeologists investigated and found chipped stone tools near the bones, as well as a few arrowheads. Several of the bison bones had cut marks from stone tools consistent with prehistoric butchery practices. These discoveries added up to a possible bison jump.

Archaeologists found hundreds of bison bones at the Nighthawk bison jump site in Texas.

"The only way bison can arrive at the site is by falling from above, as the site surface is sandwiched between two cliffs," the researchers wrote. Indigenous hunters likely used the cliff's natural spur shape to herd the bison to their deaths. "Instead of a stampede toward a surprise fall, Nighthawk could have operated more like 'walking the plank,'" according to the researchers.

Even more surprising than the discovery of a bison jump site in the southern Plains was the length of time the jump was used.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

A series of radiocarbon dates revealed that there were at least seven mass bison kills at Nighthawk over a span of three millennia, between roughly 1550 B.C. and A.D. 1550. One of these events, which the researcher named Kill 3, was responsible for most of the bison bones. That enormously successful hunt most likely took place around A.D. 300 to 400 and would have required an immense labor force and precise coordination.

Archaeologists excavating a bison jump site called Nighthawk in Caprock Canyons State Park in the Texas Panhandle.

"Bison jumping is a complicated community effort," Costa said. "Large scale bison harvests (like jumps) are exciting because they require a large group of people working together to be successful."

It is not entirely clear what the Indigenous hunters were doing with the bison killed in the hunt. In the northern Plains, archaeologists have long assumed that bison jumps were generally performed in the fall and used to provision the community for winter. Bison in the North were used to make pemmican, a shelf-stable mix of dried meat and rendered fat.

But although pemmican was an extremely useful foodstuff and trade good in the North, it was likely too warm in Texas for bison fat to last more than a few weeks, the researchers wrote. This may mean that the southern Plains bison hunts were more useful for displaying power and building alliances.

All of the kill events at Nighthawk were at least a century apart, with an average of 500 years between each bison jump. That points to an infrequent use of the jump but also a clear memory of its utility.

"The simplest explanation for long-lived jump facilities is that these techniques were passed down over long time spans rather than revived again and again," the researchers wrote.

Costa, A. G., Houk, B. A., Lyle, A. S., Bement, L., Lintz, C., Lawrence, K. L., Frederick, C. D., & Culleton, B. J. (2026). The Nighthawk bison jump: New evidence for recurrent Late Holocene bison jumping in the Southern Plains. American Antiquity, 1–28. https://doi.org/10.1017/aaq.2026.10229

Kristina Killgrove is a staff writer at Live Science with a focus on archaeology and paleoanthropology news. Her articles have also appeared in venues such as Forbes, Smithsonian, and Mental Floss. Kristina holds a Ph.D. in biological anthropology and an M.A. in classical archaeology from the University of North Carolina, as well as a B.A. in Latin from the University of Virginia, and she was formerly a university professor and researcher. She has received awards from the Society for American Archaeology and the American Anthropological Association for her science writing.

#6244. How This Creepy Critter Evolved Its Way to Surviving on Blood Alone

A blood-only diet resulted in these tiny bats rewiring their metabolism in some truly surprising ways.

Misunderstood and often maligned, vampire bats are saddled with a reputation akin to that of Nosferatu and Dracula just because they feed on blood. But unlike the vampires of movies and folklore, they don’t drain their victims. These tiny creatures couldn’t possibly hold all the blood that’s inside the much larger mammals they feed on after dark. Still, they can still consume a seemingly supernatural amount because their stomachs are built to expand.

Because vampire bats only feed on blood, they’re the only obligate sanguivores among mammals and, in fact, among all tetrapods—since their wings are modified forelimbs, they still count as four-limbed animals. When night falls, they fly out to forage, sometimes drinking up to half their own body weight in blood, thanks to those expandable stomachs and kidneys that quickly get rid of excess fluid. The problem is that blood is a poor diet. It’s mostly water, with plenty of protein but potentially toxic levels of iron, and only traces of sugar and fat. Even so, it’s the only food vampire bats will ever know. Once the young of all three living species are weaned off milk, they switch entirely to blood. They start sinking their teeth into unsuspecting victims, mostly sleeping livestock, which feel little more than a mosquito bite.

Evolutionary genomicist Michael Hiller of the Senckenberg Research Institute in Frankfurt, Germany, wanted to learn how these fascinating creatures are genetically programmed to live on blood alone. He and his research team set out to identify the changes in genes and gene expression that made this possible. They analyzed the genomes of the common vampire bat (Desmodus rotundus), the hairy-legged vampire bat (Diphylla ecaudata) and the white-winged vampire bat (Diaemus youngi), and compared them with the genomes of other bat species. By analyzing gene expression in six major organs, including the stomach, they found several anomalies. Vampire bats’ stomachs were so different from those of other bats, and other animals, that they were almost a different organ entirely.

“Extreme dietary specializations impose strong and persistent selective pressures in nature, forcing organisms to reconcile severe nutritional imbalances with existing physiological and metabolic constraints,” Hiller and his colleagues wrote in a study recently posted to the preprint server bioRxiv. “Deciphering how genomes adapt to such conditions reveals general principles of the evolutionary processes that remodel metabolism and physiology.”

Among the roughly 30,000 known tetrapod species, dependence on blood, known as obligate sanguivory, has evolved only once. Because blood offers so few calories for its volume, vampire bats have to drink large amounts of it. Because it also contains so little sugar, the bats have low baseline insulin levels and release little insulin after a meal. Some aspects of this metabolic situation resemble type 2 diabetes in humans, so studying these bats could lead to better treatments in the future. Much like fictional vampires, vampire bats also need to feed often. They have a very limited ability to store fat and glycogen, so they can starve if they go 48 to 72 hours without a blood meal. To prevent this, bats that have fed successfully sometimes regurgitate blood for roost mates that haven’t eaten that night.

The genomic shifts behind vampire bats’ sanguivory include changes in genes for digestion, metabolism and immunity, as well as the loss of bitter taste receptors. The vampire bat stomach in particular has adaptations found only in these three species. Its enlarged size is linked to three upregulated genes. These genes are also thought to play a role in the bats’ unusually shaped gastric glands and in extra connective tissue that makes such huge expansion possible. Most mammals use stomach acid to digest food, but vampire bats’ genes for producing gastric acid are suppressed. Digesting so much blood would take an enormous amount of acid, and the specialized mucus lining their stomachs leaves them vulnerable to acid damage. So over the course of their evolution, their stomachs shifted from digesting food to absorbing it.

Adaptations elsewhere in the body also help these winged vampires survive on their unusual diet. Insect-eating bats have an enzyme for digesting insect sugars that their vampire relatives lack. Vampire bats get hardly any sugar, so they have no need for it, which fits with their low insulin output. Vampire bats have also lost several genes that control gut movement in other species, but that matters little for an animal whose diet is a single liquid with little, if any, indigestible material. Similarly, having fewer fat-digesting enzymes is no disadvantage, since blood contains hardly any fat. Meanwhile, genes for coping with blood’s excess iron are enhanced. Vampire bats also rely more on their intestines to absorb amino acids and on their kidneys to reabsorb them, which keeps amino acids from being lost in urine.

Studying genomes and gene expression across several organs together was key to these findings. “This integrative approach was essential for obtaining a comprehensive view of the molecular changes associated with sanguivory in vampire bats,” Hiller said. “More generally, our work demonstrates how genome-wide, integrative analyses can yield molecular insights into the evolution of adaptive traits.”

#6243. Global Airlines Is “Fyre Festival”, Not Virgin Atlantic

Yesterday, a Hi-Fly charter airplane took off from Glasgow bound for New York, with Hi-Fly crews and pilots. If you read the papers, it was purportedly ‘Global Airlines’ maiden flight, even though there’s no regularly scheduled service, the pilots and crew weren’t theirs, they couldn’t legally sell airline tickets on their own website and they don’t have a license to operate.

In 2025, crazy things are par for the course, so that didn’t stop all sorts of promising headlines of a revolution in the skies. This is the airline that promised stunning innovation and joy in the air, and the press gave Global Airlines an early gift, by comparing the story to Richard Branson and Virgin Atlantic. That’s just insane, as you’ll soon read.

In reality, anyone can charter a plane and have Hi-Fly operate it, and anyone foolish enough can pay extra for a custom paint job with their logo, or more financially insane — buy a scrapyard A380 and be on the hook for its maintenance, while paying a third party to fly it.

The whole ‘Global’ pitch was that people love the Airbus A380, hate all the current global airline experiences ( really?) and airline services — and a revolution in the skies, can happen again. It sounded exciting. We all like to dream. Global’s first flight would be the testament to what air travel can be and something passengers love. So, how’d they do?

When Virgin Atlantic launched in 1984, the airline industry had been in a massively “beige” management consultant style, joy killer phase for a decade.

The fun “golden era” aircraft spaces and frills of the 60’s had largely been stripped out and bus travel comparisons were totally fair. Richard Branson’s light hearted approach to service and differentiated selling could shift dollars and votes — and measurably did.

Let me be very clear: that simplicity in differentiation is no longer the case. You cannot shift wallets and put butts in seats just by saying you have a cool airplane alone, or a bar on board (particularly when it’s just a beverage cart that says pub).

From leading (actually real) global airlines, passengers expect, at minimum, the following…

When “Global”, and by Global I really do legally, technically mean Hi-Fly the jet charter company which actually flew the scrapyard plane that “Global” bought, they did NOT have…

Travel blogger Noel Phillips shared some of the trip with his following. The following screen grabs are…. cute?

The truth is, Virgin Atlantic didn’t have nearly as gargantuan of a task in the 80’s as any airline coming to market does today. In the 80’s many airlines were stuck, did lack innovation and had a pool of largely uninspired talent, with no experience outside of the airline vertical. There also wasn’t this whole technology thing, as standard expectation.

That’s all so far from the case these days and most that are specialized in the airline world are wickedly sharp. Most new people I know at airlines now also come from major tech companies, other travel verticals or impactful innovation firms.

Airlines are getting pretty good at this ole’ air travel thing.

A differentiated approach to smiles on board and a little bit of extra focus on fun, food and drinks could really shift minds and mentalities in the 1980’s, but now you gotta back it up, baby.

Everyone likes to feel special and Virgin, forever, has made people feel special at a time without tech. I’d argue Virgin has taught Delta a lot about that, and it’s a contributing factor to Delta’s rise as a premium airline. It didn’t happen overnight, and what looks easy never is.

Getting people to fly with you is now about safety, reliability, excellence in mobile technology, schedule and personalization. Then fine, we can care about which champagne; or caterer or lounge style or airport, and which celebs like it. Yes, these legacy airlines can appear stuffy at times, but my god, can you not marvel at the technology revolution making air travel journeys excellent?

On real airlines, before I even arrive at the airport, I can use the NFC chip in my passport pressed against my phone to validate my document and bypass human interaction. I board a United, or any serious airline flight nowadays and see a notification that my bag is loaded onto a cart to be loaded on the plane, then again when it’s loaded onto the plane!

I hit the wifi and I’m connected sitting at the gate. If for some reason the flight is at all delayed, or connection in jeopardy, I can instantly rebook onto any other service at no charge, without talking to a soul, with just a tap on the app.

Their seag back screens have blockbuster movies, boxsets and everything else you could want for a one hour, or 15 hour journey. It’s all just standard now, not innovative.

The app navigates me through the airport and even tells me when my zone is boarding. AKA – stand the “f” back. The food is at least solid, the beverages are getting better because of their scale (buying power) and there are fewer poor customer service interactions because of how tech forward and seamless journeys are.

All the great, big airlines do this. This is like… baseline for a real player.

Tell me, or ask the Global Airlines CEO, James Asquith, where in the roadmap all of these essentials are? I want to make it clear that their priority for the last three years was a Soho House press conference about serving champagne in economy, maybe, “if they could get the economics right” rather than any of these basic things.

And in the end, they didn’t even deliver on the silly things they prioritized. The first Global flight wasn’t a remotely differentiated take on economy, business or first, as promised. It was 12 year old seats from another lackluster airline, without real refurb and even the long haul dignity of any seat back entertainment, which that airline which scrapped the plane offered.

If Richard Branson was at the helm, they never would’ve let that flight take off. Making a splash means at least doing one thing differently, right? An airline promising total innovation, A380 experience and differentiation cannot launch a flight which does not even meet the basic standards of budget carriers like Norse. You just can’t take off. You innovative something!

Let’s not forget that when Richard Branson formed Virgin Atlantic, he’d already founded a notable brand and number of businesses in the UK, was quite famous, and filed records and company books in a place where they are scrutinized. He was “real”, even if some was bluster. The public could and did use his businesses.

James Asquith’s only claim to fame, other than from the Instagram account he bought followers for, to fake fame — yes, factually — is that he was the “CEO” of Holiday Swap. Omg, so big time!

The business purports to be a home swap company, though there are no financial records of any legal merit in the West, and despite my damndest multi-year attempts, no record of actual customers. Simple use of Similar Web or review sites will help your own conclusions. You can read old blog posts for more musings. The rumors of what laundered through are scary. Maybe a real journalist can find out for us?

I actually think it’s dangerous to the public to compare these two people.

I’ve had the good fortune of meeting Richard Branson many times throughout the years and he’s always been wildly impressive. Wickedly sharp, analytical, funny and personable. It’s easy to put in a good shift for PR purposes, but I’ve observed levels of deep dive knowledge that no setup encounter can protect for — and genuine interest too. He cares about his people and he worries about the details.

I also have many people in my personal life connected to the Virgin Atlantic founder and I know of nothing but admiration and respect for the man, his company ethos and family. Business in the front, party in the back.

My only encounter with James Asquith was when he was fuming that he wasn’t invited on an airlines press trip, slid into my Instagram DM’s wanting me to blast them – and for us to be best buds as we roast a major (actual) global airline. That airline later confidentially told me he was banned from flying, due to his antics. I politely declined and he unfollowed me. It was soooo cool.

I guess if you can’t fly other airlines, you start your own?

So yeah, if you ever feel like putting your life in the hands of an airline without functioning entertainment screens, or WiFi, or regularly scheduled service, or new seats, or a mobile app, or an actual license to fly planes, definitely fly with Global. Oh, and no viable loyalty program either. Forget about earning points from daily spending and turning them into upgrades.

Those other “boring” airlines with all the bells and whistles above are clearly not ready to make travel great, with a new golden age, again.

Gilbert Ott is an ever curious traveler and one of the world's leading travel experts. His adventures take him all over the globe, often spanning over 200,000 miles a year and his travel exploits are regularly... More by Gilbert Ott

His intrusion and snide comment ab0ut Simon Calder was entirely unnecessary. I have little respect for Asquith as it is, he doesn’t seem to actually “do” anything other than post Insta’s of slamming Champagne, and buying an Instagram account for the new venture is downright deceptive. Prove me wrong, I’m all for new carriers, but part of me wants it to fail just because of the insufferable “CEO”.

‘Global Airlines’ reminds me of the line from ‘The Producers’: “Under the right circumstances, a [person] could make more money with a flop than he could with a hit.”

This is why many say “hire for personality and train for skill.” James Asquith has failed this test with his attitude and stands little chance of building a culture within his company that can grow to compete with the likes of Virgin. I was always concerned that this airline was launching without any unique selling points at all. Now to read that what little was brought in from China Southern does not even work: it’s for me very sad to read. Substantial funding was needed to get this far and there seems to have been very little planning around the customer experience. I raised 350k externally to launch my last business, and that was not easy for me to do. So to imagine the capital sums that will be wasted here for all the unforced errors made, it’s so disheartening given it was foreseeable! There are so many case studies, even from Virgin with Virgin Nigeria and Virgin America to review! James Asquith seems to be very lazy and entitled. A great opportunity not afforded to many better qualified people (not me), has been thrown away!

While I agree with everything in this article, I also feel like immediately criticizing new entrants and disrupters is not fair. There is not a single person in aviation that wants to see less A380’s, that want les competition transatlantic, or fewer carriers. I appreciate Global, I appreciate BOOM, and I think it is just as sensational to criticize Global as it is for them to put on a metaphorical Fyre Fest in the sky. This is responsible reporting, but let’s also at some recognize the feat that getting this particular plane in the sky, with people, to NY was. Aviation was built on the backs of visionaries and risk-takers, I hope we will continue to celebrate that spirit.

I’m genuinely surprised that yours seems to the the only objectively credible take on this fiasco. I’ve watched a couple of the first flight review videos and the aircraft and service are laughable, yet the internet is still awash with “great to see!” and “Go Global!”, all blindly ignoring the current capabilities of the competition summarised above as if they don’t matter.

At least it’s given us a good laugh over the last few years but someone is losing money (hard to call anything sunk into this shambles an “investment”) and I imagine the flag carriers will be delighted as it makes them look stellar by comparison. Got to seriously question the judgement of anyone that wanted to get involved with Global. It’s all been smoke and mirrors from day one.

#6242. Math’s holy grail, the Riemann hypothesis, appears solved with AI’s help

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

The proof apparently settles a 167-year-old question related to prime numbers

The Riemann hypothesis reveals a secret order hidden in the prime numbers.

ROBERT BROOK/Science Photo Library/Getty Images

This is a human-written story voiced by AI. Got feedback? Take our survey . (See our AI policy here .)

A long-sought pinnacle of mathematics has apparently been reached. In a feat that will go down in mathematics history, a human working with AI appears to have solved the most famous puzzle in math, proving the Riemann hypothesis. The problem has foiled repeated and valiant attempts at solution for more than a century.

Now, mathematicians are working to understand the proof, posted by Levent Alpöge, a mathematician at Anthropic, on November 20. The Riemann hypothesis, if true, reveals the secrets of prime numbers. In a statement on his website, Alpöge said he’d developed the proof alongside Anthropic’s AI tool Claude.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

By the next day, independent mathematicians had confirmed the result. “We have full confidence that Alpöge’s proof of the Riemann hypothesis is correct, and we congratulate him on this achievement,” read a joint statement from Lean Focused Research Organization and Mathlib Initiative.

A proof of the Riemann hypothesis is one of the most sought after achievements in mathematics. “As a mathematical landmark, it really doesn’t get bigger than this. I can’t think of a theorem proven not only in my lifetime, maybe in the history of mathematics that is as important as this,” says mathematician Ken Ono of Axiom Math and the University of Virginia in Charlottesville.

“It’s an historic achievement,” says Bryna Kra, a mathematician at Northwestern University in Evanston, Ill.

Importantly, this was not the work of AI alone, Kra says. First of all, Claude had been trained on the work of thousands of human mathematicians, plus Alpöge was an experienced mathematician himself. He did not just ask for the proof then “push a button and wait,” Kra says.

Over six weeks, he worked back and forth with Claude. As an AI agent, Claude can use outside tools to perform tasks. The precise version of Claude that Alpöge used has not been disclosed, but the AI checked its work using Lean, software that converts mathematical arguments into code in order to confirm that a chain of logic holds up. It also had access to Mathlib, a library of known arguments already converted into Lean.

The result is 250,000 pages of dense, complex math. The world’s mathematicians are still working to translate the proof into a form people can understand. “What’s amazing about this proof is that it involves so many different areas of mathematics,” Ono says. “And I don’t know how a single human being could hold all of the ideas in their mind.”

The Riemann hypothesis, which dates to 1859, is closely linked with prime numbers. Prime numbers seem to be sprinkled randomly along the number line, but the Riemann hypothesis reveals a hidden order. At play is a mathematical enigma called the Riemann zeta function. The zeros of this function — the values that, when plugged into the function, produce a zero — are closely related to prime numbers. The Riemann hypothesis says that certain zeros — of which there are an infinite number — all sit on a particular line on a graph. If that is true, it would reveal how many primes exist below a given number.

Because so much of mathematics involves prime numbers, many other mathematical statements rest on the correctness of the hypothesis. The new proof will have wide implications. “It’s an earthquake throughout mathematics,” Ono says.

Alpöge claims to have solved not only the Riemann hypothesis itself, but a more general form of it, called the generalized Riemann hypothesis, which extends the idea to related functions. Though he guided the AI, Alpöge wrote that “what I saw during the course of progress so amazed me that I believe it is one dawn across science of something far greater … Claude far outpaced me near the finish line.”

AI has been steadily felling major problems of mathematics, and this is the biggest one yet. But according to cognitive scientist Gary Marcus of New York University, AI’s genius at math will not carry over to more open-ended types of problems in biology, business or robotics. “In short, it’s not at all obvious that whatever Alpöge did has the generality many people are hoping for,” he wrote in a Substack post.

And some mathematicians have pushed back against the dominance of AI, disputing the utility of proofs created with the technology. The Association for Human Mathematics wrote in a November 20 statement on their website that no human being can claim to be responsible for the Riemann hypothesis proof, and that no mathematician can “confirm with full certainty that the proof is correct.”

Kra has been critical of achievements where AI agents worked largely on their own, independent of human intervention. The recent solution, by OpenAI, to a puzzle about the Navier-Stokes equations that describe fluids came about that way. But Alpöge’s approach was different, Kra says. “There is someone to stand behind [the work],” she says. She just hopes that people don’t see this as an end to math. “I think that this is a beginning, this is opening up more questions than it answers. … I think we have to use our imagination and find what’s the next frontier.”

Astronomers once assumed galaxies were born before black holes, but giant black holes spotted in the early universe are forcing them to rethink their order of events.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Nearly every large galaxy is thought to have a supermassive black hole at its center. The Milky Way's black hole, known as Sagittarius A*, is enormous, weighing over 4 million times as much as the sun. But which came first: the black holes or the galaxies around them?

Astronomers told Live Science that they thought they knew, but new observations mean they're no longer sure.

For decades, the prevailing idea was that galaxies came first: Dying massive stars leave behind black holes that can merge and feed until they swell to millions of times the sun's mass, said Joseph Silk, an astrophysicist and professor at Johns Hopkins University.

Then, in recent years, the James Webb Space Telescope (JWST) began peering back at the early universe. "Recent observations are challenging this picture, or at least showing us that it cannot be the whole story," Roberto Maiolino, a professor of astrophysics at the University of Cambridge, told Live Science in an email. "We are finding extremely massive black holes just a few hundred million years after the Big Bang."

The galaxy GHZ2 (white box) contains the oldest known supermassive black hole. Discovered by the James Webb Space Telescope in 2022, its light had to travel some 13.4 billion years to reach Earth.

Stranger still, some of these black holes look too big for their hosts. In nearby galaxies, a central black hole is typically about a thousand times less massive than its galaxy, Maiolino said, but some early ones "appear to be almost as massive as the stars in their host galaxies." In a study in the journal Nature, Maiolino and colleagues measured one such black hole's mass directly in an object called Abell2744-QSO1 and found that it holds most of the object's mass.

So where could such giants come from? Maiolino outlined several possibilities, and more than one may be correct. Some supermassive black holes may be ordinary stellar remnants that grew much faster than usual. Others may have been "born big," forming from the direct collapses of enormous gas clouds, which "would give the black hole a head start in its growth," Maiolino explained. Another idea is that these monsters were seeded by primordial black holes that formed "shortly after the Big Bang, before the first stars and galaxies existed."

Further complicating the question is that black holes and galaxies also push and pull on each other. A growing black hole can release an enormous amount of energy that heats or expels gas, which, in turn, curbs or shuts down star formation, Maiolino said.

Feed your curiosity with an exclusive mystery every week, solved with science and delivered direct to your inbox before it's seen anywhere else.

However, it can also compress gas and potentially trigger new stars. "Black holes and galaxies influence one another throughout their evolution, and neither can be understood entirely in isolation," he said.

A black hole spewing jets inside the elliptical galaxy Centaurus A.

Silk said the balance varies. In giant, elliptical galaxies, black holes weighing billions of suns can have "histories of extreme violence" that helped limit their hosts' growth, while in spirals like the Milky Way, feedback from stars tends to dominate.

So which came first? Answering that question will take far more data from JWST. Right now, "we have samples of tens of objects, maybe 20, 30, 40," Silk said, and astronomers need far more data to tell whether oversize black holes are typical.

If black holes outweigh their galaxies the farther back astronomers look, that would strongly suggest black holes formed first, Silk said; if stars dominate, it would point the other way.

Maiolino suggested the question itself may need rethinking. "Asking which came first may be too simplistic," he said. "The more interesting question may be how black holes and galaxies formed, grew and influenced one another at different stages of cosmic history."

There may be no single sequence. "Different black holes, in different environments and at different cosmic epochs, may have formed and evolved through different pathways," Maiolino added.

For now, the cosmic chicken-and-egg puzzle remains open. As Maiolino put it, astronomers are "beginning to explore a period of cosmic history for which we still have many unanswered questions."
