#6229. The 8 Best Headphones for Giving Your Ears the Treatment They Deserve

Our handpicked, tested sets start at around $100.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

The fact of the matter is that it doesn’t take a lot of work to find a good pair of headphones these days. After decades of competition and high-tech design, the market is saturated with dozens of high-quality options at every shape, size, and price point. Whether you’re looking for a basic set of earbuds for less than $100, or would prefer to drop $300 to $500 on a pair of wireless ANC headphones with high-tech bells and whistles like support for lossless audio files, or even want to spend top-dollar on a pair of wired, audiophile-grade cans to plug into an immaculately constructed hi-fi system, you won’t be short on choices.

Over the past five years or so, there haven’t been many game-changing innovations in the audio space, but that has led to a flattening of the field that’s great if you’re looking for a bargain. Features that would have once been considered high-end, like active noise cancellation, have trickled down into budget products, and audio quality has been steadily improving among budget- and mid-tier headphones. There are benefits to buying a high-end pair, for sure, but there are more bargains than ever before.

Obviously there are hundreds, if not thousands, of headphones out there—more than even I can test. I’ve put in a lot of time, though, going over the best, the most interesting, and the most talked about headphones, to find the ones that stand out from the pack. Because even when there are a lot of good options out there, we all would rather bring home the best.

I’ve been professionally testing tech products and audio gear, especially headphones and earbuds, since 2011. When I evaluate headphones, I spend weeks and, in some cases, months using each product as my daily driver, assessing its sound, battery life, and ergonomics. I pair the headsets with phones and laptops and frequently switch between devices.

My test routine included streaming an eclectic selection of tracks from Apple Music and Qobuz to evaluate each headset's ability to produce audible bass, treble, and mid-range. I also listened to podcasts, streamed videos, and played video games while evaluating each pair of headphones.

To put the headphones’ noise cancellation through its paces, I wear them on the New York City subway to get to work, in the large open office I share with my colleagues, and on long-distance flights. I make calls, too, carefully observing if their microphones help participants hear me clearly.

I monitor the battery performance of all wireless headphones by tracking how often I have to charge them. I want to ensure that every pick’s battery life at least matches its manufacturer’s claims.

Because you may wear your headphones for long stretches each day, I carefully scrutinize the size, fit, and ergonomics of every pair by using them for hours between breaks. I also evaluate the layout and reliability of their controls, whether they are buttons, touch-sensitive surfaces, or a combination of both.

With that guidance in mind, find your next favorite pair of headphones among the thoroughly tested and reviewed sets below.

If I had to part with all my headphones and keep just one pair, I’d choose the Technics A1000. These wireless headphones are my new benchmark for all-around excellence, blending an elegant yet understated design, supreme comfort, and outstanding audio performance. That includes high-fidelity sound and efficient noise cancellation on par with the industry’s best offerings.

Featuring sophisticated magnetic-fluid audio drivers, the Technics A1000 headphones impressed me with balanced, detail-rich, distortion-free sound right out of the box, faithfully reproducing everything I listened to during testing — from music and podcasts to video content. Instrumentals in my eclectic jazz selection sounded crisp and vibrant. On my favorite downtempo albums, the bass was deep, while the vocals were superbly defined and perfectly separated.

The Technics companion app gave me a rich set of tools to customize the headphones’ sound and noise cancellation. Depending on the music I was listening to, I could adjust the bass and treble levels and tweak the mid-range output to my liking, using a graphic equalizer or pre-loaded presets.

In a mandatory comparison with identically-priced rivals like the Sony WH-1000XM6 and the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) — a duo of products with superior button controls, longer battery life, more futureproof Bluetooth 6.0 connectivity with the ability to simultaneously link to three devices, and full Dolby Atmos audio capabilities with optional head tracking. The last point is a step above Sony’s proprietary, multidimensional 360 Reality Audio, which is more cumbersome to access.

We’ve reached a point where a pair of wireless headphones from a reputable brand with elegant design, high-quality sound (including spatial audio), stellar noise cancellation, and long battery life costs over $400. By offering some of these features for $200, the Nothing Headphone (a) over-ear cans are the biggest bang for the buck and worth the attention of value-obsessed gearheads.

Design- and durability-wise, the Nothing Headphone (a) makes similarly priced rivals look generic by comparison. The headphones’ rectangular ear cups with rounded corners give them the same distinctive look as pricier offerings from the same maker. These include transparent and solid-color bits that give the headset unique character. Their IP52 water- and dust-resistance rating is also remarkable, as it’s rare for over-ear headphones at any price point.

Amazing hardware button controls that include roller and paddle keys, as well as a customizable one, are another reason I became a fan of the Nothing Headphone (a) and all other headsets from the brand. Their responsiveness and tactility are better than products that cost twice as much.

On the audio front, the headphones delivered enjoyable, slightly bass-forward sound and immersive spatial audio. The Nothing X app offered intuitive tools to customize my listening experience, and I liked the option to link the cans directly to my devices via a USB-C or a standard audio cable. The cans’ noise cancellation was also solid, if not on par with the serenity offered by more expensive competitors.

The 75-hour maximum battery life with noise cancellation alone is reason enough to put the Nothing Headphone (a) on your radar. I didn’t have to worry about recharging the headset for weeks. Turning noise cancellation off almost doubles the battery life, bringing it to a staggering 135 hours between charges.

Bose headphones and earbuds have been synonymous with noise-canceling excellence for decades, so it’s no surprise the brand’s QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) over-ear cans are the first product that comes to mind if this feature is a priority. Of course, the headphones are also stylish, supremely comfortable, and deliver top-notch sound, including immersive spatial audio.

Regarding noise cancellation, I wouldn’t recommend the headphones solely for their ability to eliminate ambient noise distractions quickly, since that’s a given in this price range. What gives the Bose product an edge over any rival in this department is the option to customize the noise cancellation by choosing from eleven levels of intensity, then saving it into a custom mode for specific activities (e.g., work, travel, commuting, etc.) that’s easy to access by long-pressing a button.

Having a quick-access mode with maxed-out noise cancellation for work and travel, another where the feature’s intensity was set below 50% for my daily subway rides, and one with full ambient awareness at the tip of my right thumb was super convenient with the Bose headphones. Plus, I could include spatial audio in my custom modes.

During months of use, the QuietComfort Ultra headphones delivered powerful, entertaining sound, customizable via their companion app. Their spatial audio capabilities are just as impressive, and I tip my hat to Bose for making proprietary Immersive Audio technology, with or without dynamic head tracking, available on any content, not just Dolby Atmos-enhanced music and videos. That said, if audio fidelity is your top priority, you’ll likely prefer the identically priced Technics EAH-A1000 or the Sony WH-1000XM6.

Calls sound superb on the QC Ultra 2, as usual. I like the headphones’ control layout, with clicky buttons and a volume touch slider that doubles as a customizable key. The QuietComfort Ultra’s 30-hour battery life with noise cancellation is far from best-in-class, but ahead of the previous version and more than enough to keep you tranquil on any flight.

We live in times when most consumers think of headphones as bulky over-ear headsets, and that’s what makes the Marshall Milton ANC special. These headphones offer features and performance you’d expect from a larger set—top-notch sound customizable via an app, reliable noise cancellation, and long battery life—in a more compact, lightweight package with an on-ear fit and scratch-resistant ear cup covers better suited to on-the-go use.

Sound-wise, the Marshall Milton ANC impressed me with crisp, energetic sound that you can customize via a companion app. Its noise cancellation is also stellar, though the headset doesn't deliver the same level of tranquility as a top-shelf over-ear pair. The extra layer of passive noise isolation such headsets provide is instrumental. Still, the Milton ANC makes up for it with a lighter and more comfortable fit.

The headphones’ knob and customizable button are excellent and miles ahead of many competitors’ control layouts. So is their 80-hour maximum battery life without noise cancellation. If you like the Milton ANC’s design and controls, but want an over-ear set, I have good news. The Marshall Monitor III ANC headphones offer similar design and controls in an over-ear form factor with a slightly higher price tag.

Review: Marshall Milton ANC Wireless Headphones

The Soundcore Q31i wireless headphones by Anker are your best bet if you want to stay in two-digit price territory. Believe it or not, for under $100, you can get a reliable set with a comfy fit, solid audio performance, good noise cancellation for the price, futureproof connectivity, and price-defying battery life in a choice of three colors (black, white, and pink).

Acoustically, the Soundcore Q31i headphones performed better than their price tag suggests. The sound was surprisingly harmonious out of the box and customizable via the feature-packed app. While I wouldn’t ditch my expensive headphones for the Anker offering, I found its sound super enjoyable. Their support for Hi-Res audio in wired and wireless mode was a particularly nice touch that felt unthinkable at this price point.

The headphones’ noise cancellation is adequate, if far from the best in the business. I didn’t get the same silence as with more expensive products, but I had no trouble focusing at our large open office when I put the headphones on. The key feature, like the sound, is adjustable in the companion app.

Overall, the Soundcore Q31i exceeded my expectations when I put it through its paces. The lack of spatial audio is my only gripe with the headset, but at $60 on sale, it’s nowhere near a dealbreaker.

Audio-Technica’s ATH-M50x is the first option that comes to mind when someone asks me to recommend a pair of wired over-ear headphones that offer top-notch sound, commendable ergonomics, and impeccable brand cachet, all at an agreeable price. The legendary maker’s product ticks all these boxes, so whether you are looking to take a break from Bluetooth or need a reliable tool for work, or to enjoy, say, your vinyl collection, it is an excellent buy.

A consistently balanced, high-fidelity sound is among the many reasons why many audio engineers and audiophiles swear by these Audio-Technica headphones. My favorite aspect of their audio performance is its accurate and enjoyable bass depth. Countless wired and wireless headphones, especially in this price range, are heavy on bass but nowhere near as proficient in producing mid-range and highs, which is why I always keep the ATH-M50x in my rotation.

The headphones’ retail package is as rich as their sound. It includes three cables of various lengths and a soft pouch. Due to their immense (and well-deserved) popularity among consumers, Audio-Technica ATH-M50x headphones have an excellent ecosystem of third-party cables, cases, and ear cup covers.

If what I told you about the ATH-M50x piqued your interest, but you prefer wireless headphones, I have good news. Audio-Technica offers a Bluetooth version of the cans. The Audio-Technica ATH-M20x headphones, on the other hand, are a great option for upgraders on a very tight budget.

The Technics EAH-AZ100 wireless earbuds offer the same blend of acoustic excellence and onboard features as the brand’s over-ear headphones I mentioned, but in a sleeker, lighter package with an in-ear fit and a lower price tag. These qualities make the buds my top pick in their crowded product category. I’d take the Technics offering as my sole set of earbuds over any big-name rival.

Equipped with magnetic-fluid audio drivers, the EAH-AZ100 delivered pristine, distortion-free sound across countless listening sessions. The harmony among bass, mid-range, and treble fully met my high expectations. The buds’ spatial audio output, with full Dolby Atmos support and optional head tracking, was equally impressive. Their call performance was also stellar.

The earphones’ ability to tune out ambient noise matches their audio fidelity and is rightfully among the industry’s best. Thanks to passive noise isolation from their comfortable ear tips and sophisticated hardware, I had no trouble blocking out distractions when I needed to. The companion app let me choose between fully adaptive noise cancellation based on my surroundings or a desired level of noise cancellation.

Like the Technics over-ear headphones, I compared the EAH-AZ100 buds with their direct competitors: the Bose QuietComfort Ultra (2nd Gen) and the Sony WF-1000XM6. In this group of elite options, the Technics set earned my nod for offering (arguably) better Dolby Atmos-certified sound, longer battery life, and simultaneous connection to three devices. Noise cancellation is equally great across all products, though I’d give Bose an edge for offering custom settings for specific scenarios. Lastly, this might sound like nitpicking, but the EAH-AZ100’s charging case is sleeker and fits more easily in the small pocket of my jeans than its rivals’.

Bowers & Wilkins has sterling credibility among discerning audiophiles — the folks who obsess over high-fidelity stereo sound with precise separation between left and right channels and are willing to spend big on gear that delivers it. The British audio maker’s Px8 S2 wireless headphones should top the wish list for this group of gearheads, offering a listening experience similar to its luxury speakers in a pair of over-ear headphones.

Listening to the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2 headphones felt like being in a private space with a hi-fi system. Their out-of-the-box stereo sound captivated me with its accurate presentation, as intended by the content’s audio engineers. Depending on the song and genre, I could hear lively vocals, crisp instrumentals, and deep bass without opening the companion app to tweak settings. By contrast, their strong noise cancellation put me in a cocoon of silence, letting me focus solely on the music.

Of course, the Bowers & Wilkins app gave me plenty of options to customize the cans’ sound and even activate an immersive spatial audio mode. However, I liked the original sound so much that I kept it as-is most of the time, whether wired or Bluetooth.

In a manner befitting their price category and brand heritage, the Bowers & Wilkins Px8 S2 deliver style and craftsmanship in spades. The headphones are made from a mix of leather, metal, and fabric, so they look and feel luxurious. Their comfort and button controls are equally impressive, fully meeting my lofty expectations after months of testing.

Before we dig into hardware specs and features to keep on your radar, know that spending more on your next Bluetooth or wired headset will get you better audio performance across the board and more onboard features. By audio performance, I mean noise cancellation, support for immersive spatial audio, and superior call quality, among other essentials. These features require sophisticated onboard processors and multiple integrated microphones, which inevitably reflects the retail price.

Many budget cans support lossless audio formats, but you shouldn’t prioritize this unless you have a top-shelf Android phone that supports audiophile-grade LDAC and Qualcomm AptX codecs. Lossless audio also isn't available on Spotify, so make sure your streaming service supports it. Apple Music, Amazon Music, Tidal, and Qobuz are a few that do.

If you’re shopping on a tight budget, I suggest spending $80 to $100 for a good pair. The most feature-packed wireless noise-canceling headphones cost north of $400, so budget accordingly if you want one. You’ll find your investment well worth it when you turn on noise canceling and discover it’s like a mute button for your surroundings.

Due to their lack of Bluetooth chips, batteries, and additional components to control noise cancellation, spatial audio, and other features, wired headphones can treat you to better stereo sound quality than equivalently priced Bluetooth models. Their makers can use more capable, better-tuned audio drivers while keeping the price reasonable without those extra bits, so you can score a high-quality pair from a big-name brand for less than $200.

On the other hand, if ultimate high-fidelity and craftsmanship are priorities for you, prepare to spend a hefty four-digit sum to get what you need. Paired with an amplifier and lossless streaming, high-end wired headphones can help you (literally) discover new tones and layers in songs and albums you’ve listened to hundreds of times before. To be clear, though, only the most dedicated audiophiles should even consider something like that.

The headphones’ audio drivers deliver sound to your ears. The materials used in their making and their tuning are more important than their size. Translation? More expensive headphones feature more sophisticated drivers, resulting in higher-quality sound with a more palpable balance between bass, treble, and mid-range.

After more than a decade of headphone testing, I can confirm that cheaper models often hide their sonic deficiencies behind heavier bass. A booming low end can affect treble and mid-range production, reducing the quality of the sonic experience even if it still sounds entertaining.

Multi-dimensional spatial audio has become a standard feature on most high-end wireless headphones. By making the sound effects feel as if they come from distinct directions instead of just your left, right, and center, headphones with this lifelike functionality will make you feel like you are in the studio with the artist, part of the audience when streaming a live album, or in the onscreen action.

Better yet, the best wireless headphones with spatial audio have sophisticated onboard tech that can process standard audio into immersive multi-channel sound, including the option to add dynamic head tracking for a truly lifelike experience. As its name suggests, this feature shifts the sound source as you move your head for an even more natural listening experience.

This feature is a must for a new pair of wireless headphones in 2025—and you no longer have to pay top dollar for it. Once reserved for premium headsets, the functionality is available across the price spectrum, including under-$100 territory. It utilizes microphones and a processor integrated into the headphones to detect ambient sounds and then deliver audio that cancels those sound waves out.Noise cancellation will reduce auditory distractions during your commutes, travels, and workday. Don’t buy Bluetooth headphones that lack it, even if your budget is below $100. Naturally, spending $200 or more will give you superior noise cancellation, often resulting in near-total silence on top-shelf sets.

I typically suggest wireless headphones if you’re looking for an upgrade, not only for offering cable-free convenience but also for desirable features like noise cancellation, spatial audio, and app controls for customizing those. Look for wireless headphones with Bluetooth 5.2 (or higher) on board. These are the most futureproof wireless connectivity standards. Don’t worry if your device doesn’t support them. They are backward-compatible with older Bluetooth standards.

Wired headphones deserve your attention for their rock-solid connection to hardware, which provides instantaneous sound transmission with zero latency. Measured in milliseconds, latency is the time it takes for audio to reach wireless headphones from the source—your phone, tablet, or TV, for example. It’s imperceptible in most cases.That said, a zero-latency wired link can come in handy for video-editing projects, where the audio and on-screen content have to stay in perfect sync. The same goes for competitive gaming, where every millisecond counts.

Opting for a cable-toting set of headphones also frees you from charging, companion apps, and firmware updates. By lacking electronic components and degradable batteries, wired headsets also last longer.

Don’t settle for a wireless noise-canceling headset that can deliver less than 20 hours of battery life, as it might not be enough to get you through a super-long flight. The over- and on-ear sets I recommend here will last at least 30 hours between charges, and that’s my minimum requirement in 2026.

Still, since superior noise cancellation and fancy spatial audio tax the headphones’ battery, I didn’t mind charging the Sony WH-1000XM6 and Bose QuietComfort Ultra (Gen 2) to get a better experience than what their lower-priced rivals offered. The same goes for the Apple AirPods Max 2.

If you are shopping for wireless earbuds, a double-digit maximum battery life of at least 10 hours between charges from the bundled charging case is preferable, but not mandatory. Top-tier AirPods and Bose earphones can’t reach this milestone, but they are still easy to recommend for their excellence in other areas.

Except for AirPods and Beats by Dre products, which benefit from Apple’s superb hardware integration, any new pair of wireless headphones must come with a companion app. This includes Beats products, which can play nice with Android phones just as well as they do with an iPhone. It lets you control them and keep them up to date with firmware updates.

And look for a hard-shell storage case when shopping for Bluetooth headphones. It will keep them intact when you toss them in a bag or backpack on your way to work, or stuff them into a carry-on suitcase when traveling. No need to fret if your headphones come with a soft pouch for storage, though; just keep them at the top of your bag while packing to avoid potential (if highly unlikely) damage.

November's full Beaver Moon rises on Tuesday, Nov. 24, giving us a preview of the spectacular Christmas Eve supermoon coming next month.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Editor's note: This article was updated on Tuesday (Nov. 24) to indicate that the full Beaver Moon rises tonight.

November’s full moon, known as the "Beaver Moon," will rise in the east at dusk tonight (Nov. 24), marking the first of three consecutive supermoons.

It will be the third and final full moon of fall in the Northern Hemisphere and the first in a series of unusually close full moons that includes December's spectacular Christmas supermoon — the closest full moon since 2018. These bright moons are just some of the many winter skywatching highlights headed our way in the coming months.

The Beaver Moon gets its name from the time of year when nocturnal beavers in North America traditionally build dams and prepare for winter under the full moon, according to TimeandDate. Other nicknames include the Frost Moon and Snow Moon, and the Anishinaabeg people in North America call it Baashkaakodin Giizis — the Freezing Moon — according to the Center for Native American Studies.

The moon will reach its full phase at 9:53 a.m. ET on Tuesday, when it will be below the horizon in North America. The best time to see the Beaver Moon is at moonrise that evening, as it rises in the east around the same time the sun sets in the west. That's when the moon will appear against a relatively bright twilight sky, making it easier to appreciate its size and color.

The moon will appear full on Monday and Wednesday as well, but Tuesday offers the best opportunity to see it rise during twilight.

The Beaver Moon will be the first of three consecutive supermoons, according to EarthSky. A supermoon occurs when a full moon coincides with the moon being relatively close to Earth in its elliptical orbit. The moon's distance from Earth changes throughout the month. On average, the moon is 238,900 miles (384,472 kilometers) from Earth. When a full moon occurs near perigee, or its closest point during its orbit, it appears slightly larger and brighter than usual. Here's what's coming up:

November's Beaver Supermoon is just the beginning: It's the smallest of the three upcoming supermoons. December's full Cold Moon will be the closest, biggest and brightest full moon of 2026, bringing the moon closer to Earth than at any time since Jan. 2, 2018, according to late astrophysicist Fred Espenak.

#6227. Extinct, long-legged grasshoppers walked on water alongside dinosaurs

Every print subscription comes with full digital access

Amber fossils preserve tiny paddles on the lower leg that could have powered each stroke

Ancient grasshoppers with spindly legs glide across water in this illustration, similar to how they may have scooted nearly 100 million years ago.

Nearly 100 million years ago, spindly legged grasshoppers may have scooted across water like modern day water striders. The clues are in the fossilized insects’ legs and feet.

Special hairs and leaf-shaped leg adornments, exquisitely preserved in amber, suggest the insects — members of a newfound family of insects — could balance and slide around on surface tension, researchers report November 24 in Proceedings of the Royal Society B. The discovery suggests at least three insect groups evolved independently to move across water.

We summarize the week's scientific breakthroughs every Thursday.

Paleontologist Chunpeng Xu and his colleagues first encountered the strange insects while studying a collection of 99-million-year-old amber. Frozen in time were three pieces of amber containing wingless grasshoppers with short bodies and incredibly long, skinny legs. Due to their unorthodox body shape, Xu didn’t recognize them as grasshoppers at first and thought they might be harvestmen or stick insects.“I was genuinely amazed,” says Xu, of the Nanjing Institute of Geology and Paleontology in China. “They are among the most bizarre insects.”

Under the microscope, two details stood out: Front legs with water repellant hairs and rear lower legs with leaf-shaped paddlelike structures. Estimates of the insects’ weight show they could have ridden on the water’s surface tension, with help from the repellant hairs on their legs and their spread-out footprint across the surface of the water. And the paddlelike lower legs would have propelled them forward.

The researchers named the insects Hydrelcana zhangi, placing them in the new family Hydrelcanidae.

“Walking on water is a pretty rare skill in nature,” Xu says. Until now, only two insect groups were known to have evolved to live on the water’s surface: water striders and their kin, and a similar looking but unrelated, long extinct family called Chresmodidae.

The grasshoppers had a different gait from other water-walking insects. The common pond skater (Gerris lacustris), by comparison, rows with its middle limbs.

And whereas modern water-walking insects are predators and scavengers, the ancient grasshoppers were also probably herbivorous, given their mouthparts and lack of claws. The researchers found nine of them preserved in the same amber chunk, suggesting the insects may have gathered in large numbers to feed. It’s possibly the earliest record of such swarming behavior in grasshoppers or crickets, the team says.

#6226. One Small Kitchen Mistake Shattered My Baking Dish. Let This Essential Tip Save Your Next Holiday Dinner.

Experts recommend understanding the risks of the glass cookware you’re using.

Gear-obsessed editors choose every product we review. We may earn commission if you buy from a link. Why Trust Us?

Here’s what you’ll learn when you read this story:

I clearly remember the very last time I used one of my reliable old pyrex baking dishes, and it makes me blush. I was making a chicken recipe but had forgotten to add enough liquid to the pan. In the interest of saving time, I took the hot pan out of the oven, opened a carton of chicken stock from the fridge, and tipped a little in. That’s when my pyrex baking dish shattered into three or four large glass shards, mingled with the now ruined chicken. It broke apart the moment the cold stock touched the hot glass.

Though I was shocked, I realized what my mistake was—the glass couldn’t bear the sudden temperature change. But it made me wonder: wasn’t pyrex designed specifically to hold its structural integrity under just these kinds of temperature fluctuations? When I started searching, I found that people have been complaining about their pyrex cookware exploding for years. Perhaps they just weren’t reading the instructions. Then, I stumbled across a different reason for my destroyed dinner: there’s pyrex, and then there’s PYREX.

The first experiment to use PYREX for cooking took place more than a century ago, in the kitchen of Corning Glass Works physicist Jesse T. Littleton, whose wife used a sawn-off glass battery jar to bake in the oven. It was made of borosilicate and that was the key. Used today in cookware and lab equipment such as beakers, Corning’s “Nonex” glass was invented for hot, burning-oil railway lanterns that needed to stay intact when exposed to cold weather. Calling it fire-glass, the company later named it PYREX®, a play on the word “pyro,” meaning “fire” in Greek, and “ex,” from the label that identified its earlier product.

Since then, PYREX has withstood the intense temperatures and harsh chemical onslaughts of laboratory work. It works well for temperatures of up to 425 degrees Fahrenheit in household kitchens.

The secret to the original PYREX’s heat resilience is its borosilicate composition, a glass made of silica and boron trioxide. Glass expands when it’s hot and contracts while cooling. Heat causes its atoms to vibrate and move apart, weakening the glass. However, boron atoms don’t vibrate or separate as much as other elements, making the overall glass more stable.

Around the 1950s, Corning also began making PYREX bakeware out of tempered soda lime glass, according to Smithsonian magazine. In 1998, Corning sold its consumer product operations to Borden, later renamed World Kitchen, then Corelle Brands. Corelle continued to produce the tempered soda lime bakeware in America—this is called “pyrex,” all lowercase. These days, Corning only makes PYREX borosilicate labware products, such as beakers, for scientific use. In Europe, the brand International Cookware still makes borosilicate cookware.

✅ To have a more accurate idea of what you're buying, here’s a good rule of thumb: “Pyrex” is a brand name with clear distinctions depending on how it’s written. Only cookware marked “PYREX”—all uppercase—is likely made of borosilicate glass. However, most of this is made in Europe; lowercase pyrex brand cookware made in the U.S. has been tempered soda lime for decades. It’s still possible to locate some Pyrex brand borosilicate cookware in the U.S., but it’s harder to find. If you see the label “pyrex,” it definitely means the glass is made of tempered soda lime.

Despite its deep roots in American kitchens, home cooks have been complaining about pyrex shattering in the oven or during rapid temperature changes since the early 2000s. In 2010, the nonprofit organization Consumer Reports released a warning following a yearlong investigation of pyrex shattering incidents. “When we examined 163 incidents in detail, we discovered at least 42 reports of injuries. While hundreds of millions of dishes are used safely each year, we believe the situation is serious enough that we have asked the Consumer Product Safety Commission to investigate,” according to the report.

During testing, soda lime glass shattered at lower temperatures than “more expensive” borosilicate Pyrex bakeware, the report continued. Consumer Reports found that the iconic glass bakeware produced in America today is of soda lime, while the European-made products investigators tested were borosilicate.

Consumers also complained that the manufacturer’s instructions were confusing. Consumer Reports found that the small print on the back of products containing the necessary precautions is “easy to miss.”

Borosilicate glass can withstand up to three times as much thermal shock as soda lime silicate. “When glass bakeware does shatter, consumers report, it can break into sharp shards that go flying, raising the risks of injuries. This contrasts with claims from one of the manufacturers that its glass bakeware breaks into ‘relatively small pieces generally lacking sharp edges,’” according to the report.

Soda lime glass is made of about 60 to 75 percent silica, 12 to 18 percent soda, and 5 to 12 percent lime. Heat-treated and then rapidly cooled on its exterior, the outside of tempered soda lime glass solidifies more quickly than the center. While cooling, the inside pulls at the stiffer exterior layer, creating tension that makes the whole piece more durable. If it does break, tempered glass forms rounded, cube-shaped chunks, instead of the sharp shards of untempered soda lime glass—think about the last time you dropped a drinking glass.

Untempered soda lime glass is used for items that aren’t supposed to be heated, such as drinking glasses and windows. It isn’t safe for either the oven or the microwave oven.

So look for a European provenance, or simply “borosilicate” in the description before you buy your next glass baking dish. I know I will, because I’m pretty sure I’ve only ever owned the soda lime version.

#6224. A Woman Left Her Belongings in Pompeii Nearly 2,000 Years Ago. Archaeologists Just Found Them.

A Pompeii resident’s wardrobe and other personal affects were frozen in ash, offering a snapshot of a personal beauty routine from 79 C.E.

In a centrally located home in ancient Pompeii’s Via dell’Abbondanza (translated as Street of Abundance), one woman curated a cozy—and intimate—dressing room, obscured by a façade. The identity of the woman is itself now obscured and lost to time, but the eruption of Mount Vesuvius in 79 C.E. froze her personal habits and routines in ash. 2,000 years later, archaeologists found it exactly as it was.

The house in question likely belonged to Cornelius Maxium, based on inscriptions no longer visible but seen during a 1912 excavation. Archaeologists recently ventured behind the home’s façade, and in doing so, opened a wardrobe last opened in 79 C.E.

Archaeologists spelled out the find in an online excavation journal from Pompeii Sites, highlighting how the investigation revealed the woman’s personal beauty routine and daily habits. The wardrobe contained cosmetic tools of tweezers and a mixing palette, a glass perfume vial, an incense burner, and a bronze oil lamp. The excavation also revealed vessels and pots of bronze, glass, and ceramic, as well as a small wooden box contained lead weights, which were likely used in trading.

“Pompeii is not just a place of great works of art; it is also a place where the most ordinary objects reveal the human dimension of the past,” Gabriel Zuchtriegel, director of the Pompeii Archaeological Park, said in a translated statement. “The value of this discovery lies in the ability to piece together various traces of a life—personal habits, work, and memories. While we cannot reconstruct the identity of the house’s inhabitant with certainty, these fragments bring us closer to their daily existence.”

The woman whose wardrobe this was, for example, may have had a great affection for pinecones. In addition to the discovery of a small jug decorated with a pinecone motif, there was also a necklace with at least 24 miniature charms made from faience, bone, glass paste, and rock crystals. Some of those charms also depicted pinecones.

Tucked inside a cloth pouch inside the wardrobe, archaeologists may have found the most personal item of all: a necklace with amulets known as “crepundia,” which literally translates to rattles. Typically worn by children for ritual protection—the amulets were thought to contain spells that offered protection—the items also audibly rattled so adults could better track their children’s movements.

Roman-era experts said adults often kept childhood crepundia as a keepsake. “The Roman world was characterized by a high degree of geographical mobility at every social level, from slaves to wealthy merchants,” according to the statement. “As a result, many people found themselves living far from the parents, relatives, and the places where they had grown up.”

Amidst the personal items at Via dell’Abbondanza, archeologists may have located the woman’s proto-piggy bank, as excavations revealed a woven container holding 38 bronze coins.

That such deeply personal items, to say nothing of the hoard of bronze coins, were there within the wardrobe to be found centuries later suggests that the owner, whoever she may have been, fled the eruption and subsequent devastation with no time to extract them, and never returned to retrieve them. That, of course, is assuming they survived to even attempt it.

It’s possible the owners were not home at the time of the eruption, as the room housing the wardrobe appeared to be under some level of renovation when the disaster occurred. Even in its mid-reno state, however, the room featured expensive Italian paintings, highlighting the potential wealth of the occupants that match the prime real estate along one of the ancient city’s main thoroughfares. The excavation also uncovered the remains of some of the home’s smaller residents when Vesuvius rained down its devastation. There was a pair of young wood mice skeletons inside an amphora on the home’s mezzanine level, showing that even the finest urban homes in Pompeii clashed with rodents. Evidently, there was no crepundia warding them off.

Scientists are perplexed at discovering the world's deepest explosive volcanic eruption at Challenger Deep in the Mariana Trench.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

A submersible mission to the deepest ocean trench on Earth has made a shocking discovery: the deepest pyroclastic volcanic flow ever found on the planet, in a place geologists didn't expect to see any volcanic activity.

This evidence of a violent undersea eruption was found 20,000 feet (6,000 meters) below the ocean surface on the walls of the Challenger Deep, the deepest point of the Mariana Trench and the deepest part of the ocean. It was a "complete surprise," said Robert Stern, a professor emeritus of geosciences at the University of Texas at Dallas and first author of a new study describing the discovery.

Typically, volcanic activity doesn't occur that close to an ocean trench, Stern told Live Science. And given the site's extreme depth, the lava that made the flow must have had some very strange chemistry. Normally, the intense pressure of seawater at these depths would prevent an explosive eruption, instead favoring a goopier, seeping type of flow. But the flows seen on the edge of the Challenger Deep were similar to the explosive, roiling gases that coated Pompeii in ash in A.D. 79.

"It's not something that as a geoscientist I would have said would be predicted," said Sune Nielsen, a geochemist at the University of Lorraine in France who was not involved in the study. "Very far from it."

A fish in the genus Pseudoliparis in an image taken during during a dive by the Jason/Medea ROV at 20,659 feet (6,297 m).

The Challenger Deep is in the remote western Pacific at the southern end of the Mariana Trench. There, the Pacific oceanic plate pushes under the Mariana oceanic plate in a process called subduction. At the trench where the two plates meet, the ocean floor plunges down 6.8 miles (10.9 kilometers). Mount Everest could fit in the chasm, with room to spare.

Geoscientists aren't sure why the trench is so dizzyingly deep, but they have turned up some clues. For instance, there is a tear in the Pacific Plate that allows one narrow strip of the plate to subduct particularly rapidly. The curvature of the plate is also very steep, perhaps because the rocks of the Mariana and Pacific plates aren't very strongly connected to each other, allowing the Pacific Plate to dive steeply and flex freely.

The new findings, reported Monday (Nov. 23) in the journal Frontiers in Earth Science, suggest that volcanism and magma also may play a role, Stern said. The researchers were exploring a segment of the Challenger Deep's forearc, a roughly 120-mile-wide (200 km) expanse that sits between the trench itself and the volcanic arc created by the subduction zone. These volcanic arcs are standard subduction zone features; for example, Mount St. Helens and Mount Rainier are part of the volcanic arc of the Cascadia subduction zone in the Pacific Northwest.

Get the world’s most fascinating discoveries delivered straight to your inbox.

But though there are some volcanoes north of Challenger Deep along the Mariana Trench, the Challenger Deep segment of the trench is odd in that there is not an organized volcanic arc there. Instead, there's an ocean ridge. Regardless, the space between this ridge and the trench was expected to be volcanically quiet because there is not usually enough heat in that region of a subduction zone to melt magma.

Nevertheless, the cameras on the deep-diving remotely operated vehicle Jason/Medea, which went to the site in 2014, caught strange, pancake-like rock features at three different spots in a 60-mile (100 km) stretch of the trench. Samples brought on board the ship revealed rock embedded with volcanic glass and a pyroclastic flow texture.

A sea cucumber in an image from the Jason/Medea dive at 12,726 feet (3879 m).

The researchers are currently getting the rock dated, but volcanic glass usually erodes quickly in the ocean, Stern said, so the presence of glass suggests the eruptions were fairly recent. "They're not yesterday," he said, "but I don't think they're a million years old."

The pressure of the water at the depths of the flows is equivalent to 592 atmospheres of Earth stacked on top of one another. Typically, that kind of pressure keeps a lid on the dissolved water and carbon dioxide in magma that expands rapidly to cause explosive eruptions. Thus, Stern said, the eruptions by the Challenger Deep may have been driven by a supercritical fluid ‪—‬ a weird state sort of in between a gas and a liquid.

"We just don’t know how those magmas will behave at those water depths," said Stephen Self, a volcanologist at the University of California, Berkeley, who was not involved in the study.

The mission's observations also suggest that the crust of this region is extending, or stretching, in two different ways. To the east, the stretch is caused by a mechanical pulling apart of the crust. To the west, volcanic eruptions are stretching the crust. It's a perplexing finding, Nielsen said, without a clear explanation.

Stern and his colleagues suspect that the two plates are starting a new subduction zone in this western part. That would be an exciting finding; subduction zones move around over tens of millions of years, and researchers don't know much about how new ones start. The geochemical studies of the rocks that Stern and his team pulled up could answer questions about where the lava that made the pyroclastic flows came from and why this bizarre region can generate magma where none should be.

"This region is really, really unusual for our planet, and there is quite a bit of, 'What, really? Wait, how is that? OK, yeah, I guess maybe.'" Nielsen said. "So obviously, I find it super interesting."

Stern, R. J., Pujana, I., Anderson, M. K., Chin, E., Dygert, N., Harigane, Y., Le Roux, V., Leybourne, M., Ohara, Y., Okumura, T., Segee-Wright, G., & Etheridge, E. (n.d.). ROVing in the deep: Tectonic and magmatic complexities of the challenger deep forearc segment, southern mariana convergent margin. Frontiers in Earth Science, 14, 1929806. https://doi.org/10.3389/feart.2026.1929806

#6222. Scientists Simulated What May Happen If a Nuclear Bomb Goes Off in Space. The Fallout Is Terrifying.

Radioactive waste and resulting collisions would inflict the most damage as 98% of our satellites—and the tech that relies on them—would be wiped out.

If hypothetical aliens ever search for technosignatures, thousands upon thousands of satellites orbiting Earth should be an obvious sign that intelligent life exists on this planet. The problem is that an alien spacecraft might be better off keeping its distance. As the spiral into dystopia here on Earth continues, there has been growing concern that someone could take out many of those satellites (and the infrastructure they support) with a nuclear weapon. What would happen in the wake of such an attack is a question keeping scientists from sleeping at night.

When a team of researchers from Princeton and the University of Wisconsin-Madison gauged the theoretical destruction of a nuclear strike in low-Earth orbit, or LEO, the results were grim. There have been over 13,000 satellites at altitudes under 1,242 miles (2,000 km) since early 2026. Many of these fly close together in a region of about 193-232 square miles (500-600 km2), and the use of LEO has only been expanding as the U.S. Department of Defense continues deploying hundreds more for detecting missiles and carrying out military communications, but they have only become more of a target for hostile forces. In an unnerving thought experiment, the researchers worked out the aftermath of detonating a one-megaton nuclear weapon 311 miles (500 kilometers) above the South Atlantic—they found it would easily wipe out about 98% of satellites.

“Radiation-disabled spacecraft remain in orbit but are assumed to lose maneuverability,” they said in a study recently posted to the preprint server arXiv. “We follow collisions and breakup fragments in altitude bands, retaining mass and allowing fragments to move above and below their birth altitude after a velocity kick. Both intact objects and debris descend under atmospheric drag.”

This is not the first time a “what if” like has been batted around, in theory or otherwise. Nuclear paranoia decades ago led to an actual experiment that revealed the potential horrors of detonating something in LEO. On July 9, 1962, the the Starfish Prime test saw a 1.4-megaton bomb detonated in the Pacific, around 400 km above Johnston Atoll. An artificial radiation belt was created by clouds of electrons released from radioactive debris scattered by nuclear fission. It caused severe damage to satellites that were either in outfit at the time or launched soon afterward. Radiation continues to be dangerous long after the initial explosion, because spacecraft continue to pass through it as they orbit, experiencing degrading effects that make them more difficult to maneuver. They then end up at increased risk of collision.

The researchers found that the worst effects from a detonation over the South Atlantic would be from exposure to radiation damage, which would disable 25% of the fleet in not even a day. That would rocket to 78% after three days and 98% after a week. Damaged satellites prone to crashing would collide with each other—or scraps of space junk—and gradually shut down services that rely on them. There would be three collisions within 15 days and double that by 30. Smashing spacecraft would also clog LEO with fragments that would put even more satellites at risk, and at least 19 collisions would occur a year after the detonation. Atmospheric drag would reduce the hazard by removing disabled spacecraft orbiting lower, but those at higher altitudes would remain at the highest risk. Disabled satellites would continue to die off.

Starfish Prime was so disastrous that the Partial Nuclear Test Ban Treaty was signed by the U.S. and the Soviet Union a year later. This enforced an outright ban on testing nuclear weapons anywhere but underground, whether it was on the surface, in the atmosphere, or deep in space. Satellites in LEO have multiplied since the 1960s. How long radioactive ions can keep letting electrons loose above the atmosphere is still uncertain, but satellite breakdowns would be staggering. It would take decades to restore the damaged spacecraft and infrastructure.

“Restoring orbital services would require more than replacing the lost spacecraft,” the researchers said. “New satellites would need to survive the remaining radiation and debris. The prospect of rapid infrastructure loss followed by years of disruption reinforces the need to prevent the deployment and use of nuclear weapons in space.”

#6221. Scientists Found a Mushroom That Shouldn’t Exist: It Makes Psychedelics and Deadly Toxins

With this forbidden ‘shroom, the trip to Wonderland is only one way.

Magic mushrooms get their magic from psilocybin and psilocin, psychedelic compounds that warp reality and open portals to other realms. They have also been used by Indigenous Mesoamerican and South American peoples for centuries to induce visions. Though it was once thought that mushrooms were either magic or poisonous, there is one newly discovered species that, because of a bizarre turn in evolution, produces both psilocybin and lethal amatoxins, possibly as a defense against being eaten. That’s one trip you never want to take.

Galerina indica looks unassuming. Growing on rotting palm trunks in the humid swamps of Florida, this tiny brown mushroom has no fairytale spots or fantastical colors, so it seems like just another fungus bound to be stepped on. Under its dark cap is a darker reality. Matthew Smith of the University of Florida is the state’s official mycologist, identifying species that could be toxic and regularly consulting with Poison Control, and his team was searching for potentially lethal mushrooms when undergrad researcher Andrew Kunik noticed something strange. While documenting fungi, he found that handling G. indica turned it blue. This often occurs in psychedelic mushrooms. Further investigation found that, despite having this telltale characteristic, the mushroom Kunik had been analyzing had a more sinister kind of magic.

“Although the effects of psiloids and amatoxins in humans are well documented, their natural roles in the environment remain unresolved, with anti-fungivore defense being the leading hypothesis for both compound classes,” Smith and Kunik, who discovered both substances occurring in this species through mass spectrometry, said in a study recently published in Current Biology.

While G. indica did contain psilocybin, it turned out that the ‘shroom also secreted deadly amatoxins. There is no other species of mushroom known for producing both of these substances, and while trippy psiloids have been shown to have possible therapeutic properties, ingesting amatoxins is fatal because these peptides inhibit the enzyme RNA polymerase from creating RNA copies of genes, which leads to organ failure. Fungi are thought to have evolved to produce amatoxins in order to ward off fungivorous creatures such as snails and nematodes. The genes behind production of both psiloids and amatoxins are usually passed down through fungi to their descendants, but the way these genes are acquired is not always so straightforward. Previous studies have suggested they can be horizontally transferred between different fungal species.

Psiloids are known to be synthesized by a cluster of collaborative genes for which evidence of horizontal gene transfer has been found. The same is suspected of amatoxin synthesis, and though there is less evidence for horizontal transfer, it probably began with a fungal donor lineage (which may not have been the same species) that has yet to be identified. Genome analysis has shown that these and other fungal attributes were acquired by genes that were transferred from one species to another growing in the same vicinity. The genus Galerina is already infamous for amatoxins that make many mushrooms within the genus so deadly. How psiloids entered the genus remains a mystery, though just one fateful transfer could have incorporated the genes for amatoxin synthesis into these mushrooms.

What evidence does exist for the transfer of genes that produce psiloids suggests they seeped into a lineage that did not already contain amatoxins, and in a separate evolutionary event, was absorbed by a separate toxic lineage. Kunik’s discovery also revealed how unpredictable fungi can be. The blue pigmentation that is known to be a sign of a magic mushroom comes from psilocin oligomers, molecules linked together from a few repeating structural units, or monomers. Galerina indica has shown that seeing blue does not always mean a mushroom only contains psilocin or psilocybin. While the exact genes that are responsible for amatoxins in this species are still unidentified, and exactly how psiloids evolved in the Galerina genus can only be hypothesized, there is now another thing in Florida more dangerous than alligators.

“G. indica brings together in a single species the biosynthetic systems associated with both ‘magic mushrooms’ and the world’s deadliest poisonous mushrooms,” Kunik and Smith said, “providing a rare natural system for studying how horizontally acquired secondary-metabolite pathways impact organismal fitness.”

This silver pepper shaker reveals the Romans' love of the spice and the lengths they would go to procure it.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

The pepper shaker was discovered as part of an ancient Roman hoard.

Where it is from: Hoxne, Suffolk, England

In 1992, a farmer in the village of Hoxne in southeastern England was searching for a lost hammer with a metal detector when he stumbled upon a massive hoard of more than 15,000 ancient Roman coins, jewelry and tableware. Among the artifacts in the Hoxne hoard was a silver spice container in the shape of an imperial lady.

The artifact, named the Empress, is one of four pepper pots ("piperatoria" in Latin) discovered in the Hoxne hoard, according to the British Museum. The silver container stands about 4 inches (10 centimeters) tall and is decorated with gold around the woman's eyes, mouth, hair and accessories, including a scroll in her left hand. The woman's elaborate hairstyle helps date the creation of the pepper pot to the fourth century, but experts think the hoard may have been buried in the early fifth century, when Roman rule in Britain was ending.

At the bottom of the pot, which rests on a four-legged base, there is a disc that can be set at three positions: wide open, closed and partly open. The pot would have been filled in the open position with cracked pepper and then used in the partly open position for sprinkling the spice over food.

The ancient Romans were huge fans of pepper, Neil MacGregor, former director of the British Museum, wrote in "A History of the World in 100 Objects" (Penguin Books, 2010). Pepper didn't grow in the Roman Empire, so merchants procured it from India. This made it an expensive spice, and filling up the pepper pot would have been costly.

A wealthy Romano-British family likely used the pepper pot as elaborate tableware, MacGregor wrote. It is unclear whom the Empress was meant to depict, but researchers don't think it features a member of the Roman imperial family. However, the fact that she holds a scroll could indicate that she was both wealthy and well educated.

The ancient family who lived near Hoxne seems to have left its wealth behind during the breakdown of Roman rule in Britain, since the pepper pot was found in a chest that contained dozens of pieces of silverware, 29 pieces of gold jewelry, and more than 15,000 coins.

"This was the mobile wealth of a rich Roman family — precisely the type of person who is in danger when the state fails," MacGregor wrote.

#6219. This Guy Found a Security Camera’s Exact Location Using Only the Sound of Two Planes

Add the Doppler effect to the growing list of things that can be used as surveillance tools.

Geoguessr is a widely popular online geography game where players glimpse one still frame from Google Street View and then attempt to pinpoint the exact location on a world map. Many things can be helpful hints—the design of road signs, the format of license plates, specific road markings as well as surrounding trees and landscapes. However, a YouTuber named colsto took this idea to a whole new level by geolocating an incredibly grainy video by just its captured audio.

Mind you, this audio doesn’t have any useful hints. No one nearby is talking about this “da Bears” game with a thick Chicago accent, for example. But buried within the security camera’s spectrogram (visual display of frequencies over time) is a clue—two of them, in fact. To the uninitiated they look relatively innocuous two sloping lights roughly 920 seconds apart, but colsto recognized these lines as the Doppler effect signatures of a two planes passing overhead.

To start his journey toward pinpointing the location of this video, with the only limitation being it was filmed somewhere in the continental U.S., the YouTuber first turned to Automatic Dependent Surveillance–Broadcast data, or ADS-B, provided by aircraft equipment that constantly report speed, velocity, and altitude. Websites like Flightradar24 rely on this data to provide a real-time snapshot of on-going flights around the world. Colsto first cross-referenced this data and winnowed potential candidates by choosing parameters featuring two planes the right speed and the right distance away while still traveling within 920 seconds of each other. The results weren’t promising.

“That gave us…roughly 70,000 points,” colsto says in the video. “Now, adding on to all that logic, the silence filter—where that point doesn’t hear another flight between the two events—drops from 70,000 to 15,000. Even with all those constraints, there is just so much land area and so many flights that 15,000 points still meet all those criteria.”

Instead of going through each data point, ruling out why it doesn’t fit and refining the search parameters, colsto returned to the Doppler curves and revised one of the search’s original assumptions. These two curves didn’t represent a perfect Doppler curve because planes are constantly adjusting speed and heading, and that information—no matter how slight—is locked away within these two curves. So colsto modeled the Doppler curves to create a flight path that could then be checked against 15,000 possible points.

“The Doppler curve is a function of the radial velocity of the plane with respect to the observer,” colsto says in the video. “The Doppler curve would change depending on the plane geometry.”

Eventually, colsto found the exact security camera located in Oyster Bay in Long Island, New York, that captured the grainy security footage of the pixelated tree line.

“I’m trying to fear monger with this video. The odds that someone can and does actually do this is pretty slim,” colsto said at the video’s conclusion. “In reality, there’s probably one hundred easier ways to find you than this.”

#6218. Gabe Evans announces 2028 comeback bid from Boebert’s district

Rep. Gabe Evans, here arriving at the Capitol in July for a House Republican Conference meeting, lost his bid for a second term representing Colorado's 8th District. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call) (Bill Clark CQ Roll Call)

Colorado Rep. Gabe Evans, who lost reelection earlier this month, announced Monday a 2028 run from the neighboring district of fellow defeated Republican Rep. Lauren Boebert.

“Now more than ever, Colorado needs conservatives in Congress who will fight to keep our border secure, cut taxes for working families, keep boys from dominating girls' sports and locker rooms, protect our water, and make energy affordable,” Evans said in a statement.

His announcement comes less than two weeks after he lost his bid for a second term representing the battleground 8th District in the Denver area. While the race had been considered one of the most competitive in the country, Democratic former state Rep. Manny Rutinel secured victory by 15 points.

As part of House Democrats’ massive midterm gains, they flipped three seats in Colorado. Boebert narrowly lost her reelection bid in the 4th District to Democrat Eileen Laubacher, while Republican Rep. Jeff Crank lost in the 5th District.

Evans’ statement cited his ties to the 4th District, which encompasses the eastern part of the state and extends into the Denver metro area.

“From Loveland to Lamar, I’m ready to keep fighting in the 4th District, where I grew up, and where my family has lived since 1976,” he said.

The district has a deep history of voting Republican. Boebert won by 11 points in 2024 while Donald Trump carried the district by 18 points.

Evans is far from the first member of Congress to switch to a district seen as more favorable to his party. Boebert herself shifted from Colorado's more competitive 3rd District to run for the heavily conservative 4th in 2024.

The 4th District will likely be a top target for Republicans in 2028, and Evans’ campaign sought to portray him as a clear front-runner in what could become a crowded GOP primary.

“Gabe Evans will enter 2027 and the race for Colorado’s 4th Congressional District with $300,000 in campaign funds and name recognition that no first-time candidate in the district could match,” his campaign said in the statement. “Combined with his record as an Army aviator, police officer, rancher, and member of Congress, that gives him a head start in money, name recognition, and credibility before the field takes shape.”

A former state legislator and Denver-area police officer, Evans also served 12 years in the Army. He was first elected to the House in 2024, unseating Democrat Yadira Caraveo, and currently sits on the Energy and Commerce and Homeland Security committees.

Laubacher, a Navy veteran who will take office on Jan. 3, is the first Democrat elected to represent the 4th District since Betsy Markey won her lone term in 2008. In response to Evans’ announcement, Laubacher’s campaign said she would be “focused on making Washington deliver” for district residents.

“There’s real work to do: ending the war in Iran that Gabe Evans voted six times to continue, lowering the cost of groceries and fertilizer that his eight votes for the tariffs helped drive up, and protecting the rural hospitals across the 4th district he voted to gut,” Laubacher spokesperson Taylor Gillespie said in a statement.

From ancient coins to long-lost texts, archaeologists uncovered countless artifacts for centuries. Live Science asks its readers which one they'd want to discover themselves.

When you purchase through links on our site, we may earn an affiliate commission. Here’s how it works.

Archaeological discoveries can offer remarkable insights into the lives, cultures and beliefs of ancient peoples. From richly furnished royal tombs to caches of silver coins, some of the most significant finds have revealed how people lived, traded, fought, governed and died thousands of years ago.

Other discoveries stand out for their extraordinary preservation or historical significance. For example, the most expensive shipwreck on record — the 300-year-old Spanish galleon San José that's worth an estimated $17 billion — was found off the coast of Colombia in 2015 and continues to inform archaeologists and challenge governments that can't agree about its modern ownership. Meanwhile, ancient texts can provide invaluable clues about long-lost languages and civilizations. The Rosetta stone opened up the world of ancient Egypt to scholars, but researchers are still trying to decipher the mysterious Indus Valley script, one of the world's earliest urban civilizations.

Each type of discovery offers a new window to the ancient world. But which of these archaeological treasures would you most want to uncover? Vote in the poll below and let us know your thoughts in the comments.
