#6192. Beginner’s luck: Freshmen leave it to chance at House office lottery

Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira reacts after drawing the worst chip during Tuesday’s lottery for newly elected members of Congress. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

As far as birthdays go, Rep.-elect Shannon Taylor was having a pretty good one.

Crowded into a room in the Capitol Visitor Center on Tuesday morning with the rest of her freshman class, the Virginia Democrat walked up to a table with a wooden box and reached in.

“This is so nervewracking,” she said, before pulling out a chip with a “1” printed on it.

Her prize was a coveted one — first choice of office space. Every two years, incoming members of the House play a game of chance to see who can land the best real estate and who will be relegated to less desirable corners of the Capitol complex.

The room broke out in raucous applause and a standing ovation. Her new colleagues started singing “Happy Birthday.”

Not everyone was so lucky. Rep.-elect Mark Teixeira, R-Texas, pulled number 105 — the very last one. The former MLB player raised his arms in a mock celebration.

“Lets all hope for the luck of the Taylors,” said Rep.-elect Brent Taylor, R-Tenn., only to emerge with number 81.

The newly-elected members got their turn in a random order, walking up one by one to a table where deputy executive director of House Office Buildings Kornell Rancy kept watch over the box of chips.

Rep.-elect John Cowan, R-Ga., was the first to pick a number. The first neurosurgeon to be elected to Congress, Cowan wore his white doctor’s coat as he pulled number 11 out of the box.

“I wanted to do something where I’m just representing health care providers around the country,” Cowan said.

As returning members lay claim to more desirable offices made available by those who resign, retire or lose elections, the space they’ve abandoned is left for the newcomers, who are on the Hill this week for orientation. Many of them will end up in the Longworth Building, where suites can be awkward or cramped.

Not all offices are created equal, and the calculus has changed over the years. The previously undesirable Cannon Building just underwent a budget-busting renovation that lasted more than a decade, with a spacious courtyard opening earlier this year. But the coveted Rayburn Building still retains its prestige, despite repeated and dire warnings from the Architect of the Capitol about its crumbling infrastructure.

“You’re welcome,” said Rep.-elect Amish Shah, D-Ariz., after pulling a disappointing number 94.

Prior to the lottery, Rep.-elect Trever Nehls, R-Texas, was hoping for the best but had a backup plan in case his number said otherwise.

“If I don’t pick number one, I’m going to offer one of these cigars as a trade to whoever gets it,” he said, pointing to three of them sticking out of his jacket pocket. He’s preparing to take over the seat currently held by his twin brother Troy, who shares a fondness for stogies.

The office space lottery dates back to 1908, when members of the 60th Congress received their first office assignments after the completion of what would be named the Cannon Building. A House page drew names and numbers from a box, and members selected their offices from a chart, according to House Office Buildings executive director of facility operations Joe Yates, who kicked things off Tuesday with a history lesson.

The lottery now is a little more modern, with members poring over virtual office layouts and doing walkthroughs of spaces on laptops.

“If somebody had to get 105, I’m glad it was me because I am here to serve, and I’m serving my freshman class by picking the worst office,” Teixeira said. “This is low on my priority list.”

Some members announced their lucky draws themselves, while others let Yates break the news.

“Come visit me,” said Rep.-elect Chris Gober, R-Texas, after pulling number 2 from the box.

After the lottery itself, members huddled with their staff to strategize about the next steps — how to leverage their numbers and select the best suites left on the list, while also exploring layouts, paint colors and carpeting.

“First and foremost, a good layout, so we can do good work, and people can be comfortable in doing the work, and then a convenient location. Very utilitarian,” said Rep.-elect Scott Wiener, D-Calif., of his priorities.

“We’ll get a decent Longworth office,” said Wiener, who drew pick 43. “Cannon would have been ideal, but I’m happy with any office.”

Rep.-elect Manny Rutinel, D-Colo., was hoping to replicate the good luck of some of his colleagues. “I’m going to do the Shannon Taylor and Sam Forstag. It’s eyes closed, behind the back,” he said of his moves, reaching into the box. But it wasn’t enough, and Rutinel pulled number 69.

“These are not red numbers, these are not blue numbers. These are the remaining numbers, and there ain’t that many,” said Rep.-elect Johnny Garcia, D-Texas, who was among the last few people to pick. He emerged with number 75.

And when Rep.-elect Joe Strada, R-Fla., the last of the incoming members to draw, walked up to the table, the whole room cheered.

“Wouldn’t it be crazy if I picked number 1?” he joked, pulling out the last chip in the box.

#6190. Rep. James Comer launches 2027 bid for Kentucky governor

Kentucky Rep. James Comer, here talking to reporters on Capitol Hill in June, is running for governor. (Tom Williams/CQ Roll Call)

Kentucky Rep. James R. Comer, whose role as chairman of the House Oversight Committee gave him a powerful platform to investigate Democrats, including former Presidents Joe Biden and Bill Clinton, has launched a run for governor next year.

The Republican, who was just elected to a sixth full term representing Kentucky’s 1st District, is seeking to succeed term-limited Democratic Gov. Andy Beshear. Kentucky is one of three states holding off-year gubernatorial elections in 2027, alongside Louisiana and Mississippi.

In his announcement at a tele-town hall Monday night, Comey emphasized pocketbook issues, pledging to eliminate the state income tax and boost job-creation in Louisville.

“If we get that income tax to zero, people are going to have more money to spend, and we're going to be able to attract more good-paying jobs to Kentucky, which will be able to keep our best and brightest in the state,’’ he said.

As the leader of the House Oversight panel, Comer has been at the forefront in the fight over the release of records related to convicted sex offender Jeffrey Epstein. (Last week, the committee released a report concluding that the federal government mishandled criminal probes into Epstein’s activities.)

Comer is a staunch ally of President Donald Trump, who carried Kentucky by 31 points in 2024, and his hard-nosed style of politics is conveyed in a soft-spoken Southern drawl.

Known back home as Jamie, Comer has deep roots in rural Monroe County, dating back to the late 1700s. Prior to coming to Congress, he operated a farm before serving 11 years in the Kentucky House. In 2011, he was elected as the commonwealth’s commissioner of agriculture.

He made an unsuccessful run for governor in 2015, losing the Republican primary by 83 votes to Matt Bevin, who went on to win the general election. The following year, Comer easily won election to the House from his western Kentucky district, succeeding Republican Ed Whitfield.

Comer has moved quickly to consolidate GOP support for his gubernatorial bid. He already has the backing of Kentucky Sen. Rand Paul and Sen.-elect Andy Barr. Michael Adams, Kentucky’s term-limited secretary of state who’d been seen a potential contender, gave Comer an early endorsement this summer.

While Comer enters the race as the Republican front-runner, he won’t have the field to himself. Other declared hopefuls include local prosecutor Rick Hardin and distiller Charles “Bruiser” Martin, who appeared on the Discovery Channel show “Moonshiners: Master Distiller.”

While Kentucky has in recent decades grown reliably Republican at the federal level, the GOP has won just two gubernatorial elections there over the past half century. Two high-profile Democrats have already launched bids to keep the governor’s mansion in party hands: Lt. Gov. Jacqueline Coleman and former state House Majority Leader and Beshear adviser Rocky Adkins, who ran for governor in 2019.

In a statement Tuesday, the Democratic Governors Association dismissed Comer as “a job-killing, pro-war politician who looks down on everyday Kentuckians.”

#6189. How I Got My Visa to France

I’ve been in love with France ever since my first trip to Bordeaux in 2010. Friends I had met back in Thailand showed me around the area and introduced me to French culture. It was my first time in France and I loved the food, the wine, and the people.

But that love became an obsession when, after Bordeaux, I stepped out of the Paris metro and onto the Champs-Élysées. The lights, the energy, the mystique! There was magic in the air. I felt like I had known the city my entire life and I was simply returning home.

Since then, Paris has had a firm grip on my heart. Over the years, I spent countless visits exploring France and Paris in particular. I’ve run tours in the city and I spent a few months living there in 2019.

Last August, after yet another sojourn, I thought to myself, “What if I moved back?”

I was growing a bit tired of the NYC dating scene, the rising cost of living, and felt like, creatively, I was in a rut. With AI coming for creators like me and the industry changing, I was a little lost on what, career-wise, would come next.

And Paris seemed like the best place to go.

It’s cheaper than NYC, I had friends there already, I’ve always wanted to learn French, it would make a great base for exploring Europe, and I could start writing my next book there. There’s nothing like a change in scenery to get the creativity flowing!

But the question remained: how do you move to France?

After all, they don’t have a digital nomad visa, and you’re limited to three months if you visit on your regular Schengen tourist visa.

Well, it turns out that it’s not actually that hard. (And while I can only speak for Americans, I suspect the criteria are similar for Canadians, Aussies, Kiwis, and other “developed” nations.)

If you want to move to France, you have four main options:

The student visa is pretty straightforward. You need to enroll in a full-time university program and show you have enough funds to support yourself (around 600 Euros per month). A friend is currently there on this visa, as she is doing a nine-month intensive French program to become fluent. You still have to apply for the visa, but if you’re enrolled in an accredited school, you’ll likely get approved. Another benefit to this visa is that you can work part-time on it!

But this visa is contingent on being in school, so if you leave or quit, it’s voided. However, when you are done, you can change this to a “job seeker” visa, which can give you up to another six months in France (or more depending on how long your program was).

I thought about applying for the entrepreneur visa, but the application process is pretty complex and can take months to be approved. You have to set up your business in France — and that is a lot of paperwork. You have to show that your business makes money, has clients (at least one of them being French), and can support you full-time (you have to make at least the French minimum wage). They will scrutinize your assets and financials a lot and you’ll need to register your business in France and pay French taxes.

Additionally, France offers a talent visa. If you’re an expert in your field (with verifiable accreditations and accolades), this could be a good visa to apply for, especially if you plan to stay in France for a long time and want to physically work there. But, again, you’ll need to have some source of income and plan to do physical business in France. If you’re not an academic but someone in the arts, you have to show how you are going to add to the “culture of France” in some way.

While I would meet the requirements for both those visas, the process for either would have been time-consuming, and, since I’m not sure France is going to be my forever home, I decided not to go through that process.

So I went with the long-term visitor visa, officially called VLS-TS visiteur. This allows me to stay up to 12 months in France and is renewable in the country. It does come with a lot of restrictions, however: I can’t physically work here and I am not allowed into the French social welfare system.

It’s also the visa a lot of Americans (and most retirees) are coming in on. If you have passive income or retirement savings and just want to live in France, this is a good option for you. It allows you to set up a bank account and it can be renewed pretty much indefinitely.

The paperwork for this visa (which I’ll get into in a bit) essentially comes down to whether or not you can support yourself. French authorities want to make sure you won’t be a burden on the system.

My biggest question centered around whether or not I could “work” on this visa. A lot of creators and digital nomads are applying for — and getting — this visa.

But remember: you aren’t allowed to work on this visa so how are you going to work if you can’t work?

So let me take a moment to talk about “work” from a legal standpoint.

As I mentioned, there’s no digital nomad visa that allows you to work in France. And the French tax office said last July that remote work is considered taxable — but there are no official laws that say so. That’s just their opinion and there’s been no progress in codifying that opinion. In fact, my visa doesn’t even come with a tax number, so I can’t be taxed. I couldn’t pay taxes even if I wanted to.

The visa office asks how you’ll support yourself when you are in France and one of the sources of income they accept is “income from work.” I was very open that my means of support would be the income from this blog and my books.

The system there really hasn’t caught up to remote work. It still defines “work” as something you do physically that could take away a job from a French person.

So could I run walking tours in Paris? Nope. Could you work at a café? Nope.

But does writing this blog post count as work? After all, no one is paying for it. It’s a free resource. Does going to a café to work on the next great American novel count? What about my weekly newsletter that has affiliate links (that generate income) in it? Is writing that considered work?

The gray area is considerable, so the best thing to do is to talk to a lawyer. I recommend Daniel Tostado (yes, that’s his real name), one of the biggest American-French immigration lawyers in Paris. He has a huge law firm and regularly meets with government officials to clarify the rules on this. He gave me some solid advice.

For this long-term visitor visa, the application process is pretty easy. You go to the French government website, fill out your application, take the application number to the TLScontact website, and make an appointment. (France outsources the appointment process to this company, which then sends everything to the French consulate for approval.)

The main things you’ll want to demonstrate are that you have accommodation for 90 days on your application and enough income to support yourself. They just want to make sure you aren’t going to be a burden on the system. I went overboard. Here’s what I brought to my appointment:

I didn’t need the second bank account, tax returns, or W-2 (they weren’t required) but the woman at the appointment said the more proof you had the better and it wouldn’t hurt. And another friend who got this visa didn’t bring anything beyond what was asked in the application form. But I wanted to take no chances!

At the appointment, the staff double-checks your paperwork, takes your biometric data, collects the fees, and then sends your passport to the embassy for processing. Officially, it takes up to 15 days to process your visa, but everyone I know seems to get it back within a week.

The worst part was not knowing if you are approved until your passport is returned. While you can track the progress of your application, you don’t know the verdict until your passport is back in your hands. While I was waiting (and anxiously spiraling), I looked on Reddit and found that most denials were for lack of income or issues with their accommodation, which seem to be the two most important things to have perfect on your application.

Once you get your visa back, you can enter France any time after the start date. After you enter, you have 90 days to register your visa with the state (they give you a little QR code with instructions). This allows you to “officially” be on this long-term visa. (It’s a more paperwork kind of thing.)

Once that is done, there’s nothing else to do and you can stay in France (and Europe) until your visa expires!

So, if you’re considering moving to France, these are your options. But, as always, I’m not a lawyer and this is not legal advice. In regard to work and other issues or questions, it’s important that you seek legal counsel and get their expert opinion!

#6188. What Republicans don’t know about Black voters’ resilience cost them

Sen.-elect Scott Colom speaks during a victory rally at Tougaloo College on Nov. 11. (Brandon Bell/Getty Images)

The campaign of Mississippi’s Sen.-elect Scott Colom was rightfully praised for its clever and brutal ads. The “pick another protein” spot will forever be stuck in the brains of a huge swath of Americans, especially Republican incumbent Cindy Hyde-Smith. She underestimated Colom and his team, and will soon be an ex-senator.

However, it was fitting that the Democrat’s closing message traded the edge for a solemn reminder of who and what brought him so far on his journey to his election as Mississippi’s first Black U.S. senator since Reconstruction.

The ad delivered an all-American lesson about history, born of bravery and sacrifice.

Filmed at the Jackson, Miss., home of slain civil rights leader Medgar Evers, the ad featured Colom recounting the story of Evers, a World War II veteran who survived Normandy, only to be shot in the back by a racist assassin, resentful that a Black man dared to exercise his rights as a citizen in the country he fought for.

“He was killed for helping Mississippians vote,” Colom said. “On Tuesday, use your vote and honor everyone who died for that right.”

In a state where voting is still racially polarized, it was clear that Colom would not win over a majority of white voters; he won an estimated 25 percent, better than Democrats in recent elections and cutting into Trump’s margins, but certainly not a path to victory.

Black voters in Mississippi made the difference, as they often have. With their allies in the cause of justice, they heeded the call. They showed up despite the state’s stringent and often confusing voting restrictions, purges of the voting rolls engineered by Republican Secretary of State Michael Watson (who used unverified data from a credit bureau), and the U.S. Supreme Court Louisiana v. Callais decision that led to a wave of Southern states breaking up Black-majority districts.

When the Mississippi purges resulted in “affidavit ballots” that required verification to count, as The Washington Post reported, young Black women tracked down those voters, one by one, to do everything they could to ensure voters’ efforts were not in vain.

Black voters mattered in states all over the country, but especially in the South, where low turnout has plagued Democrats, particularly in midterm elections.

Keisha Lance Bottoms was elected the first Black female governor in the country in Georgia, where Democrats won up and down the ballot. Newly elected senators Annie Andrews in South Carolina and James Talarico of Texas campaigned for and earned support from Black voters with proposals that rose above platitudes. And don’t sleep on North Carolina, where voters flipped seats the GOP tried to gerrymander into a hardened majority. The sight of hundreds of students from HBCU NC A&T State University, denied a campus early voting site, marching to the polls, must have made the ancestors smile.

In Florida and Louisiana, where Democrats had little financial support and lost their statewide races, Black voters brought them tantalizingly close to victory and energized for the contests to come.

I still don’t expect Republicans to give up the election shenanigans, done in the name of “election integrity” and color blindness but in reality designed to demoralize as much as suppress. Why try to win over a diverse electorate with an inclusive, policy-driven message when manipulating Black-majority districts can still work?

The number of Black U.S. House members in the next session of Congress will fall, offset by a few Democrats who survived in redrawn districts, including Shomari Figures of Alabama and Don Davis of North Carolina.

But you can’t redistrict a state, and you can’t skip town halls and expect tradition, support for the Confederacy and an “R” after your name to forever save you — the Hyde-Smith playbook.

"I blocked Scott Colom from being a federal judge, and you blocked him from being U.S. senator," she bragged, too soon, on election night.

Maybe she should have emphasized affordability, saving rural hospitals and serving all Mississippians, as Colom did.

What did GOP officials in those Southern red states think they would accomplish by focusing on their base and ignoring everyone else in states they were supposed to be serving?

Did they not pay attention in history class, or maybe they attended one of those post-integration private schools where an unedited version of America’s past might not have been on the lesson plan?

Did they believe that voters who remembered Evers, Fannie Lou Hamer, Vernon Dahmer and countless others would shrug and say “you win” when legislatures and elections officials quickly and cynically pounced to quiet their voices?

That would be disrespectful to all the people who worked for, sometimes died for rights they knew they may never enjoy, yet had a belief in America and the rightness of their cause.

Scott Colom and the Evers family remembered. He was emotional in his reaction, in an MS NOW interview, when asked about the statement from Reena Evers-Everette, daughter of Medgar and Myrlie Evers. “Their courage helped make this moment possible,” she said.

Colum agreed: “I absolutely stand on their shoulders. And from the bottom of my heart, I’m going to do everything I can to make them proud.”

Post-election, he has been very gracious, saying that he intends to serve all Mississippians, including the woman whom I suspect would hit a different note if the election had turned in her favor.

I have no doubt Scott Colom means it. He knows who paid the price to get him this far.

Mary C. Curtis has worked at The New York Times, The Baltimore Sun, The Charlotte Observer, as national correspondent for Politics Daily, and is a senior facilitator with The OpEd Project. She is host of the CQ Roll Call “Equal Time with Mary C. Curtis” podcast. Follow her on X @mcurtisnc3.

#6187. Don’t Visit Ko Lipe

After 19 years, I finally went back to Ko Lipe, the Thai island I spent close to a month on in 2006. Back then, it was one of those super off-the-beaten-path destinations that few but the most intrepid travelers visited, where electricity only ran a few hours a day, basic bungalows right on the beach cost something like $2 USD, and there really was a last boat for the season.

There was much to do here but that was the point. You hung out on the beach, read a book, went snorkeling, went back to the beach, drank beers at the one beach bar on the island, rotated meals between the five restaurants there, and went to bed early.

It was paradise – and a place a lot of people got stuck. Days easily turned into weeks here.

If you asked me what the highlight of all my travels was, I would be the time I spent on Ko Lipe. I made incredible friends, lounged around, got to know the locals, learned a bit of Thai, and, overall, lived that idyllic backpacker life we all dream about.

Over the years, I’ve avoided going back to Ko Lipe because the memory of my time there is so strong that I didn’t want to ruin it. Any re-visit would simply be trying to recreated a magic that couldn’t be recreated because the people that it special wouldn’t be there. I’d be chasing travel ghosts. And, since I know my sleepy paradise has been developed greatly over the years, I was also too afraid seeing that would make me sad.

Tourism in Thailand tends toward the unsustainable. No island really develops in a good way. It’s all build, build, build.

And I didn’t want to see my Ko Lipe like that.

But as I was planning my recent trip through Southeast Asia, returning to Ko Lipe made sense. I was heading down the Indian Ocean side of Thailand on my way into Malaysia and I’d pass by it.

And, since I was looking for a lively place for New Year’s Eve, it seemed liked the best choice. I knew there would be travelers there and there were no other nearby islands that would work, especially since Ko Lipe has a boat to Langkawi, which was my next stop.

And I’m sad to report that Ko Lipe took the Ko Phi Phi model of tourism and is now extremely overdeveloped.

Most of the island is now paved over, the old dirt footpaths having become concrete for the cars and construction trucks. Swaths of palm trees are now the sites of high-end resorts with pools (on an island with no natural water supply). Construction of more resorts continues at a fast pace. The coral around the island is dying, a victim of all the boats, anchors, pollution, and overfishing. Beaches are now lined with boats, their exhaust spilling into the ocean, leaving a shiny film you can see as you swim. And the restaurants cater to tourists looking for bad Western food, not great Thai cuisine.

The island’s boom has displaced many locals, who were forced to sell to mainland developers, and much of the island’s workforce is now from the mainland. They see little of the benefits this tourism boom.

So lies Ko Lipe, another victim of Thailand’s all too common overdevelopment and exploitation of limited resources.

I met lots of people there who loved the island. If it’s your first time, I can see why you would love it. After all, the area is postcard perfect, the water is perfectly an azure blue, the sand is a beautiful white, and since you’re surrounded by a national park, a lot of tours take you to some secluded islands.

And, in comparison to Ko Phi Phi, Krabi, or Phuket, it is less developed so I can’t fault someone stepping here for the first time going “wow!”

But, as I reflect on the island and its overdevelopment, I have come to the same conclusion I have about Ko Phi Phi: people shouldn’t visit.

I’m not against growth, but I’m against this kind of growth. It’s not sustainably managed and going there will only tax the island’s limited resources even further. You can’t put the genie back in the bottle and no local is going to say “sure, I’ll stay broke so you can an idealized vision of the world.”

And, with so many other islands to visit that are well managed (Ko Lanta, Ko Jum, and Ko Mook, to name three nearby), I think you should skip Ko Lipe.

A visit there will only make things worse.

It pains me to say that, because it was such a beautiful place, and my original visit had a huge impact on my life. But if we’re going to be good stewards and travelers, sometimes you just have to say enough is enough.

And Ko Lipe is a place where enough is enough.

Go somewhere else that is better managed.

Riding elephants in Thailand went away when consumers became more conscious of it. Eco lodges got big because of consumers. Overtourism is talked about by consumers as much as it is by locals.

Maybe if enough people start to do something, Ko Lipe will change.

But, at the very least, by not going you are at least no contributing to the problem.

#6186. Why This Company is One of the Best for Finding Work

Most travel is extractive and passive. You show up somewhere, take photos of the same landmarks everyone else takes photos of, eat at a restaurant the guidebook recommended, and hit up some bars. You take some tours to learn about the place and, if you’re lucky, get to meet some locals on your trip. You don’t really go deep.

Even long-term travelers who talk about how they “aren’t tourists” do the same – just at a slower pace and while trying to spend less money.

And there’s nothing wrong with that. That’s just the nature of travel. While we all imagine dropping into a place, befriending locals, and having this crazy time like we’re in some movies. But that doesn’t happen. Because we’re just passing through and, for the most part, locals don’t want to become friends with tourists. In fact, most locals don’t interact with tourists. (I mean it does happen but it’s not the norm.)

If you really want a deep travel experience, you need to stay. If you want to understand a place, you need to stay. The most transformative travel experiences I’ve ever had involved contributing something and staying somewhere long enough to build real relationships. It was being embedded in a place rather than just passing through.

I think that more travelers should give back when they travel. In the old days, it was hard to find out what organizations and opportunities were legit, vetted, and actually made the lives of locals better.

Now, there’s a ton of companies that can help you not only find meaningful volunteer jobs when you travel but also paid jobs when you travel and one of the best ones is Global Work & Travel. Use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a discount on your next trip.

Global Work & Travel is the world’s largest gap year company and has been placing people on working holidays, volunteer programs, teaching positions, internships, and more for nearly 2 decades. They’ve helped over 116,000 people and they cover destinations across, the UK and Europe, the Americas, Asia, Africa, and the Pacific.

Even for experienced travelers, moving abroad can be difficult. Finding employment as a traveler, securing permanent accommodation or getting stuck in shared rooms for months on end, transport costs in a new city, interview after interview competing against locals… This is just the beginning of what long term travelers need to consider.

Fortunately, companies like Global Work & Travel provide the scaffolding or safety net that makes working abroad possible for people who don’t want to figure everything out themselves. They handle job matching, pre-departure support, visa guidance, placement, and ongoing assistance through their gWorld portal, a personal trip management app that keeps everything organized in one place. For first-timers especially, having that support structure can be the difference between actually going and endlessly deliberating. The programs they offer span a wide range:

For the past decade, “digital nomad” has been the aspirational version of long term travel. Work remotely, earn in a strong currency, live somewhere cheaper, repeat.

But that model only really works for a small subset of people. You need a remote job, a certain income level, and often a level of career stability that most younger travelers simply don’t have yet.

Instead of bringing a job with you, you get one when you arrive. You integrate into the local economy instead of floating above it. You meet people through work, not just coworking spaces or short-term hostels. And you build a life somewhere, not just a temporary routine.

In a lot of ways, working holiday makers are having a more grounded and accessible version of what people think digital nomad life is. You’re not just passing through, you’re actually living there. You have coworkers, a schedule, a reason to stay longer than a week, and a chance to build real lifetime connections.

It’s also far more realistic for most people. You don’t need a remote business or years of experience. You just need the willingness to go and the right setup to make it happen.

That’s why I think we’re seeing a shift. Less “how do I work remotely?” and more “how do I actually live and work abroad for a year?”

And that’s exactly where structured programs like Global Work & Travel come in. They remove the biggest barriers, finding a job, navigating visas, getting set up, so people can actually make that shift from idea to reality.

For a lot of travelers, this isn’t just an alternative to digital nomad life. It’s a more sustainable, accessible, and realistic way to actually live and work abroad.

Volunteering abroad has a complicated reputation, and it’s worth being honest about that. There are lots of bad volunteer programs out there in the world. Programs that don’t really give back and are designed to make travelers “feel” like they did something but really are just profit driven campaigns. Global Work & Travel’s vets programs in the areas such as wildlife conservation, community development, education, and healthcare in the locations and countries it operates so you know the program you sign up for is legit.

The case for ethical, well-structured volunteering is genuinely strong. When you work alongside local Zanzibar communities on problems they’ve defined as priorities, or with wildlife and conservation in South Africa or Elephant rehabilitation in Thailand — something shifts in how you understand the world. Not only are you helping to give back to a place but you also understand the true needs of a the people and ecosystems living there, but also helping overcome the struggles they go through. It opens your mind and shifts your perspective.

Their Global Animal Welfare Fund also channels resources directly into conservation projects at their partner sites, so the impact extends beyond individual placements.

Working holidays let you truly experience a country instead of just visiting it. You immerse yourself in the culture by living like a local every day. You meet more people both locals and fellow travellers while building real friendships. Best of all, you get paid to travel, so you can stay much longer instead of rushing through in a few weeks. This lets you experience local life deeply, discover hidden spots, and understand how people really live in different places. You also build valuable skills, boost your resume with international experience, and make long-term travel more affordable since your income covers the costs. Plus, you gain a real cultural understanding that no short holiday can match. All that while stil getting paid? Not bad right?!

Working holidays turn travel into a true lifestyle, not just another 2 week vacation.

Global Work & Travel are the world leaders in long term travel and offer a ton of options for travelers looking to volunteer, work, or spend extended time in a destination. Some things I like about them.

Do I need prior experience to work abroad with Global Work & Travel? For most trips, generally nothing more than basic work experience is required. Teaching programs include TEFL training, and volunteering can be started from no experience.

What’s the minimum age? Most programs are open from age 18. Working holiday visas typically cap at 35 depending on the destination country but volunteer and teach programs are open to ages 18–80.

How long does the whole process take? It varies by programs and destination. Most people book their trips 6-12 months in advance for proper planning, job matching and visa quotas. You can get started for as little as $1 here.

Is my money safe if things change? Global Work & Travel and their lifetime deposit policy means your initial payment doesn’t expire. They are also members of many consumer protection services to further support travelers.

Can I go as a solo traveler? Yes, and this is actually one of the most common scenarios. The gWorld Community and programs group connections mean you’ll be meeting others in the same position quickly.

Travel has always been best when it’s been more than tourism. The moments that stay with you — that you actually tell people about five years later — are never the ones where you queued to see a famous landmark. They’re the ones where you connect with people. They are the moments where you did something.

Global Work & Travel makes doing something deep accessible in a way that genuinely wasn’t available a decade ago. If you’ve been thinking about doing something like this but the logistics have felt too complicated, check them out and use code NOMADICMATT to unlock a $100 discount on your trip.

#6185. The Right Tote Bag Is the Ultimate Travel Companion—These Are Our Editors’ Favorites

If you’re looking for a bag so versatile it can be your go-to personal item one day and your grocery shopping companion the next, the renowned tote bag is the only option. From early morning flights to daily office commutes, or even a packed Saturday afternoon at the farmers market, our editors are always relying on their favorite tote. The best tote bags hold everything from our laptops, headphones, and water bottles to sleep masks and our most-used beauty products. Whether you reach for a structured leather version to pack your essential items in or an oversized, canvas carryall for a day at the park, the functions of the right tote are infinite.

Though the design of a tote bag is inherently simple, our favorite brands have curated precise variations to suit every kind of traveler. My favorite tote has been my everyday work bag for years, but it has also accompanied me on countless flights, weekend getaways, and last-minute happy hours. A reliable tote bag really can do it all. Keep reading to discover 15 of our editors' favorite tote bags and why we can’t live without them.

Coach has been a favorite brand of mine ever since I got my first little black bag as a teenager. Though I still cherish that tiny bag, my most used Coach item is my leather tote. For years, the Nina Tote bag has been my reliable sidekick. I’ve had it for so long that Coach no longer produces it. On the bright side, the Maggie Tote bag is almost identical to mine and is just as practical. I have put my bag through anything and everything over the years, and there is very little wear and tear. The leather is structured and durable, yet flexible enough to fit everything I need without toppling over. With plenty of interior pockets, my necessities all have a place, so I never have to go digging through the bottom of my bag to find the right lip gloss. Not only do I love traveling with this tote, but it’s also my everyday work bag and my go-to for almost every kind of activity.

I've never really had a work bag that I truly loved until I tried this one from Cuyana. What I appreciate about the System Tote are the additional organizational accessories that you can purchase to add a bit more structure to the interior. Aside from lugging it to and from the office each day, I use this tote as a personal item on the plane and brought it with me on a road trip to Acadia National Park, and have found it to be the ultimate travel companion. The built-in interior pocket is perfect for storing essentials you need to reach easily, like your passport, earbuds, or some petty cash, and since the bag can be snapped closed, you don't have to worry about anything flying out. —Jamie Spain, travel bookings editor

This bag is all about the pockets. No tote has ever kept me quite as organized as this one from MZ Wallace, a brand known for its signature quilted bags. It offers six interior pockets, five exterior pockets, and a detachable pouch, offering me a dedicated space for all of my essentials plus a whole lot more. I’m always impressed at how much this thing fits; an umbrella, my 13-inch laptop, a full change of clothes, and my lunch. The Medium Metro tote features ultra-soft shoulder straps, making it a go-to for commutes to the office. My favorite thing about this bag is how lightweight it feels even when full—it never digs into my shoulders or hurts my arms. More features that make this roomy tote a smart choice for travelers: a luggage sleeve, protective feet, and a detachable and adjustable crossbody strap. —Meaghan Kenny, commerce editor

Monos’s Metro Tote has been with me longer than most New Yorkers are in relationships. I’ve had this faux-leather cutie for nearly five years now, and it’s traveled with me through new jobs, new apartments, and plenty of new adventures. I actually bring it to work with me every day—the laptop sleeve and spacious interior keep me organized on my way to and from the office. —Hannah Chubb, senior commerce editor

I've received so many compliments on this gorgeous structured bag from Cuyana—it's been a great work bag, with plenty of space for my laptop, planner, Kindle, chargers, and other day-to-day essentials. I wasn't sure how well it would function as a personal item as there's not a zipper to fully close the bag, but on a flight to Aruba, I made use of the leather ties to keep items contained, and found it well-sized to slip under the seat in front of me, even with my toiletry bag and a sweatshirt stuffed inside. I'm also a big fan of the snap-to-close key leash, and the interior slips pockets and zipper pocket. —Madison Flager, commerce director

The bag is perfect in the way a red apple sitting on a teacher’s desk is perfect. It’s classic, without ornament, the kind of thing that expresses its utility in its design. It’s both ubiquitous and aspirational, stirring up images of a dreamy East Coast: a white-sand, Nantucket beach; a shabby, wood-planked boathouse on the coast of Maine; a Gothic-inspired Ivy League campus. I've used it as a carry-on item, a beach tote, and as a weekender. Simply having it out on display in your home has the power to imbue your space with a charming, outdoorsy vibe. —Jessica Sulima, commerce writer

Baggu’s Nylon shoulder bag is more durable than its canvas tote bags but equally as stylish. It’s slightly slouchy, slightly structured, and comes in the signature Baggu colors and patterns. The adjustable quilted shoulder strap allows for a crossbody fit, a must-have for me when I’m commuting into the office or walking longer distances (nobody needs their laptop sliding off their shoulder onto the sidewalk). The zip closure and interior pockets are handy for organizing miscellaneous goodies and preventing spillage. Plus, the lightweight material can easily be flattened to fit into my suitcase. I find myself continuously reaching for this multipurpose tote on my way to the gym, office, farmers market, and airport. —Hannah Towey, associate editor

Just when I think I’ve run out of room, I haven’t. The expandable bottom of this Calpak laptop tote adds an extra four inches, allowing me to add last-minute essentials or souvenirs mid-trip. Like all products in the brand’s Luka collection, it’s made of a lightweight, ultra-soft, puffy exterior that makes carrying its handle easy. The material is also easy to clean—simply wipe away dirt or spills without a worry. Inside, there’s a padded 15" laptop sleeve, multiple side pockets, and a zippered section to keep smaller items organized. Another feature I love: There’s a zippered pocket on the outside that keeps my phone or passport secure, while still being easy to access. It’s a great tote for commuters and thanks to its luggage trolley sleeve, an ideal carry-on bag for travelers. —M.K.

As a shopping writer who is constantly running between the office, press previews, catch ups with friends and, of course, the airport, I need a bag with space for all the day’s exploits and then some. July’s Juliette Soft Work Tote is my perfect do-it-all companion. It’s beautiful—I’ve received multiple compliments on this bag as I’ve been whizzing around with it, and the divided interior is really clever. There’s a 14" laptop sleeve to keep tech protected—all the more important when you’re headed on a flight— and there’s also a dedicated water bottle holder too. It has a wide bottom so your lunchbox can go inside flat, plus a key leash to stop the rummage for your house keys. Brushed gold hardware and a buttery-soft faux leather exterior mean it looks effortlessly chic at after-work drinks, and when I'm off to the airport, the removable trolley sleeve slides over my suitcase handle so I can breeze through the terminal. It is my favorite desk-to-departure tote bag. —Charley Ward, commerce writer, Condé Nast Traveller UK

My Strathberry Kite is my most-used travel accessory. Not only do I use it for day-to-day tasks, it comes with me on almost every trip (the exception being adventure travel), and most recently carried me through trips to Lisbon and Istanbul, where I spent weekends catching up with friends and sightseeing. It's an ideal size for a laptop, should you wish to take it, but fits in plenty of other necessary items, too (like flip-flops or ballet flats after hours of strolling through cobbled streets). I love the walnut color and the soft, supple leather. I'm sure this will be a favorite of mine for years to come. —Abigail Malbon, global audience development manager

When I first saw Parker Thatch offers its Jack Tote bag in this unique zebra and burgundy color combo, I knew it had to be mine. I never travel without animal print, and there was something about this colorway that felt perfectly understated yet maximalist. I found it online about a year ago, and it sold like hot cakes—and has been (devastatingly) sold out since. I received it as a sweet gift from my partner a few months ago, who had pre-ordered it to arrive right when it was back in stock. I've been using it as my go-to work bag ever since. It has an incredible amount of space and strength to carry all of my everyday essentials and then some—from my laptop and a book to makeup and toiletries. Because of its exterior fabric as hair-on cowhide, she just needs to be shielded from the rain a bit more than your average bag. If the design is calling your name on this bad boy, it’s well worth the splurge. —Jessica Chapel, commerce writer

I love anything Longchamp, and this gorgeous beach tote from the brand is my cherry on top of any vacation outfit. It’s large enough to hold a full day’s worth of goodies (sunscreen! sweatshirt! beach read!), but fits on the shoulder with ease. Plus, the toggle on the front keeps things contained in the most Longchamp-esque way. —H.C.

After passing the gauntlet of a last-minute trip to the British Virgin Islands, I always keep the Foldie Travel Bag on me, whether it’s riding in my backpack during my daily commute or stuffed into my suitcase on longer hauls. The front pocket easily held my thick reading list and two Moleskine classic notebooks; the full 40 liters of space in the main compartment (with the expansion unzipped) fit a week’s worth of clothes, chargers for four different devices, and another bag filled with toiletry bottles, plus room to spare for souvenirs. Another perk: the two inner pockets and wet pocket proved useful in sorting out the bag’s increasingly chaotic contents. The luggage sleeve was a relieving bonus that allowed me to transfer the hefty weight of my zealous packing to my suitcase. —Kat Chen, editorial assistant, destinations

I absolutely love this tote. Whether I’m wearing it to the office or while traveling, it fits everything I need. Plus, it comes with a separate removable pouch that I use even when I’m not wearing the bag. This slouchy bag is super durable and matches any outfit. —Pooja Nayyar, associate social media manager

Sentimentality may cloud my vision, for the tote in my possession belongs to my late grandmother. And when I tell you I was complimented frequently for it while in Italy, I mean I felt I needed to use the bag to beat back admirers waxing: “Wow, is Vera Bradley back?”; “Is it reversible?!”; “The textiles are so beautiful.” I often caught myself fantasizing about dumping it upside down to perform a “What’s in my bag” for nobody in particular—so capacious is the tote that I was needlessly carrying multiple novels within and rarely remembered to leave my toiletry kit on the hotel bathroom counter where it belonged. Handy pockets ringing the interior are just icing, and would have kept my passport safely inside had I ever been moved to act on the aforementioned dumping. —Charlie Hobbs, associate editor

#6184. Some records in Ilhan Omar case will be released, judge says

Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., speaks during a news conference at the Capitol last summer. Few details have emerged so far about the government’s search of her home earlier this fall. (Bill Clark/CQ Roll Call)

A judge said he will order the release of some information about the federal investigation into Rep. Ilhan Omar, D-Minn., which included a search of her Washington house last month.

Judge James Boasberg for the U.S. District Court for the District of Columbia made the statement Tuesday during a hearing brought by news organizations and an advocacy group seeking details about the search. Boasberg ordered the government to provide him by Friday what could be disclosed in the case. He pointed to how investigators are handling the “speech or debate” clause immunity that Omar has as a sitting member of Congress.

“This is purely legal questions, interesting questions, about the privilege, the extent of the privilege and how it would apply,” Boasberg said.

The Constitution includes an immunity for members of Congress for the “speech or debate” they engage in as part of their jobs.

Boasberg also directed the government to propose redactions to the as-yet secret docket. While he said next week’s expected disclosures would not include the 67-page document that investigators provided to justify the search, he left the door open to unsealing that down the road if the government closes the case or brings charges.

Justice Department attorney Alessandra Serano argued against broad disclosures, calling it “very rare that a precharging, pre-indictment unsealing would happen.”

The high-profile nature of the investigation leaked into the courtroom Tuesday, as Boasberg cited statements by President Donald Trump and others about the investigation into Omar.

“You have had administration officials, prominent ones, talking about the purpose of the investigation,” Boasberg said.

Administration officials have accused Omar of committing immigration crimes for years, and Trump said last month the DOJ was looking into Omar “strongly.” Department of Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said on a recent podcast that investigators had served multiple search warrants and were investigating possible immigration fraud tied to when Omar entered the United States as a child.

Separately, Boasberg said he may issue rulings in the coming weeks unsealing portions of other court cases tied to the investigation, including one brought by Omar herself earlier this month seeking the return of the items seized in the search.

The administration executed the search warrant in October, just a few weeks before the midterm elections. The timing of the search drew accusations of political bias from Democrats who claimed that the administration brought the case to sway the midterm elections.

For years Trump has said he wanted criminal charges to be brought against his political foes, including Omar and others in Congress.

#6183. How the Antigravity 360 Drone Will Change Your Travels

Drones are huge. And, while there’s lots of restrictions around them, a lot of travelers take them on road because they produce some amazing sweeping aerial shots.

There’s lots of amazing brands out there but one that I think is super cool is the Antigravity A1. Released in late 2025, attempts to render the traditional gimbal obsolete for a vast segment of creators. By leveraging a dual-lens 360-degree capture system, the A1 records everything in every direction simultaneously. The result is a “fly now, frame later” experience that feels less like piloting a drone and more like directing a virtual camera in a pre-recorded digital environment.

I was sent one to use and want to share my experience and why I like this product so much.

What make’s Antigravity 360’s so special is the two lenses. Most drones feature a single lens that points forward. However, the A1 features two ultra-wide-angle lenses positioned on the top and bottom of the central fuselage that each captures a 200-degree field of view. When those images are combines, they overlap to create a seamless 360-degree sphere.

And, in the final exported footage, the drone itself is digitally removed, creating the illusion of a camera floating in mid-air with no visible means of support.

The sensors themselves are 1/1.28-inch CMOS units. While smaller than the 1-inch sensors found on some “Pro” level photography drones, they are massive compared to typical 360 action cameras. This allows for significantly better low-light performance and a higher dynamic range, capturing details in the highlights and shadows that would typically be lost in the harsh contrast of a midday sun.

Most countries require drones weighing 250 grams or more to be registered and subject to stricter flight rules. Antigravity clearly understood the importance of this threshold because they made the A1 to weigh exactly 249 grams with its standard battery meaning it’s not considered a commercial drone so you don’t have to register it.

And the drone feels remarkably sturdy. It utilizes a high-grade carbon-fiber-reinforced polymer that offers a better strength-to-weight ratio than the standard ABS plastic found in cheaper models. The folding mechanism is satisfyingly tactile, clicking into place with a precision that suggests long-term durability. When folded, the drone is roughly the size of a large smartphone, though about three times as thick.

The Vision Goggles: These are sleek, lightweight, and feature dual 4K micro-OLED displays with a 120Hz refresh rate. The latency is nearly non-existent and they have integrated head tracking. Because the drone is recording in 360 degrees, you aren’t limited to seeing what is in front of the drone. When you turn your head to the left, the goggle feed pans to the left. If you look down, you see the ground passing beneath you. This provides a sense of presence and spatial awareness that is simply impossible with a traditional fixed-camera drone.

The drone uses a single-handed motion controller. You point the controller where you want to go and pull the trigger to accelerate. Tilt your wrist left to bank, or raise the nose of the controller to climb. It is an incredibly intuitive system that allows even a novice to fly through complex environments within minutes. For professional FPV pilots who prefer the precision of manual acrobatic flight, the A1 does support a traditional “Mode 2” stick controller, but the motion controls are so fluid that most users will likely never switch back.

The marketing for the Antigravity 360 proudly displays “8K Resolution.” In a traditional camera, 8K means every pixel is packed into a 16:9 rectangle. In 360 video, those pixels are spread across a full sphere. When you “reframe” that 8K sphere into a standard flat video, you are looking at a “crop” of the total image.

The color science is noticeably improved over previous 360 cameras. The A1 features a “Vivid” profile for those who want punchy, social-media-ready colors, and a 10-bit “Log” profile for professional editors who need to match the footage to other cameras in a color-grading suite. The stabilization, powered by Antigravity’s “FlowState” algorithms, is nothing short of miraculous. You can fly in 20mph winds, and the footage remains as steady as if the camera were on a tripod.

The “Antigravity Studio” app allows you to download footage wirelessly (at speeds up to 80MB/s) and reframe your video using your phone’s gyroscope. You simply watch the video and move your phone around to “film” the scene in real-time. The app also features “Auto-Frame,” an AI tool that identifies subjects and automatically generates a cut that keeps them in focus. For a solo creator, this effectively provides a virtual camera crew that never misses a shot.

Battery technology remains the bottleneck for all small drones. The A1’s standard Intelligent Flight Battery provides a theoretical 24 minutes of flight. In real-world conditions with moderate wind and constant recording, expect closer to 19 or 20 minutes.

While 20 minutes sounds short, the “work per minute” is much higher than a traditional drone. Because you don’t need to re-fly a path to get different angles, a single 20-minute flight can yield the same amount of usable footage as three flights with a Mavic. For those who need more time, the “Pro Battery” (which pushes the weight over 250g) offers a staggering 39 minutes of flight time, though it does compromise the drone’s agility slightly.

In terms of flight dynamics, the A1 is a “cinewhoop” style flyer. It is stable and predictable rather than aggressive and twitchy. It has a top speed of roughly 36 mph, which is plenty for following bikes or cars, but it won’t keep up with a professional racing drone. The “Turtle Mode” is a life-saver; if you crash and end up upside down, the drone can flip itself over using its propellers, allowing you to take off again without a “walk of shame” to recover the aircraft.

The Antigravity 360 is a niche product that is rapidly becoming mainstream.

The Antigravity 360 (A1) is the most exciting drone I have tested. By removing the need for a gimbal and the stress of manual framing, it allows the pilot to focus on the one thing that truly matters: the story they are trying to tell.

While the image quality isn’t quite at the level of a high-end cinema drone, and the lenses are admittedly delicate, these are small prices to pay for the creative liberation the A1 provides. It bridges the gap between traditional cinematography and the immersive world of VR.

If you are a creator who is tired of the same old “drone shots” and want to push the boundaries of what is possible in the air, the Antigravity 360 is an essential addition to your toolkit.

#6182. 11 Warm-Weather Destinations to Flock to This Winter

Arguably the best way to overcome winter is to pretend like it’s not happening—i.e., jetting off to a warm-weather destination, where seasons are not taken very seriously and an outdoor adventure is always on the table. The best winter vacation destinations offer comfortable temperatures, off-peak advantages, and festive happenings. On this list, you’ll find some of the usual suspects, from Punta Cana to the US Virgin Islands, as well as locales you might not have considered (far too often, travelers forget vibrant Marrakech is a shorter-haul Mediterranean option).

Whether you’re interested in hiking to the wild and wondrous waterfalls of Puerto Rico’s El Yunque National Rainforest, snorkeling through the kaleidoscopic waters of Belize’s barrier reef, or simply want to kick back and relax with a dip in Costa Rica’s hot springs, these sunny locations are bound to cure those cold-weather blues. So, trade your snow boots for flip-flops and get to plotting your next escape.

When to go: JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

If you’ve been looking for an excuse to finally book that trip to Hawaii, shoot for after the holiday rush, when flights get significantly cheaper. January might be the start of rainy season in Maui, but the showers are often short and localized; for the most part, you’ll enjoy sunshiny days with temperatures that hover in the low-80s. Humpback whales make their way from Alaska around this time, and you can spot the giant beauties from Papawai Point on Honoapiilani Highway, an overlook facing the ʻAuʻau Channel. If you’re not afraid of big waves, heavy north swells at this time of year make for excellent surfing, especially at Ho‘okipa Beach Park. The Road to Hana, a scenic and beautiful drive at any time of year, becomes especially lush in the winter after the rain has fallen, and you’ll likely avoid the crowds too. Along the way, hit up sites like the Twin Falls or the black sand beach at Waianapanapa State Park.

Where to stay: A Condé Nast Traveler Triple Crown winner, Hāna-Maui Resort, a luxurious off-grid escape, is the pot of gold at the end of the Road to Hana, while Hotel Wailea offers an adults-only vibe on the southwestern coast. Though much humbler, Jimi Hendrix’s former gingerbread-style home, now available for rent on Airbnb, is also a fair contender for your home away from home, surrounded by all kinds of fruit trees and perfectly positioned for daily rainbows.

When to go: December–JanuaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While you won’t be breaking a sweat in San Diego come December, it’s an excellent place to escape to around the holidays for festive fun in mild, mid-60-degree temperatures. The Parade of Lights is a classic seasonal event, when over 100 private boats get decked out in twinkling lights and sail around San Diego Bay (watch from spots like Shelter Island or Seaport Village on select nights in December). Between November and January, you can also enjoy ice skating without the chill at the Hotel del Coronado, where you’ll glide alongside the Pacific. They say San Diego sunsets are best in the winter, when the sun cuts a path closer to the horizon and there’s not as much coastal marine fog—one of the best places to catch one is Sunset Cliffs Natural Park on the Point Loma peninsula.

Where to stay: La Valencia, otherwise known as the “Pink Lady” of La Jolla, is one of San Diego’s most iconic stays, and you might hear a seal or two barking in the distance. For unparalleled mountain views, consider this glass house overlooking Sweetwater Regional Park.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 70–85 degrees

For a Caribbean escape with outdoor adventure, cultural festivals, and farm-to-table splendor, head to Puerto Rico. From December to March, you can take advantage of the dry season on the island, which means your days won’t be interrupted by sudden showers. Holiday festivities continue well beyond Christmas, from Three Kings Day on January 6—the oldest of these celebrations takes place in Juana Díaz, with a reenactment of the Magi on horseback—to the San Sebastian Street Festival, when the namesake street in Old San Juan is filled with art vendors, live music, and plenty of mofongo (January 21–24 this year). Winter is also a great time to explore El Yunque National Forest when it’s not shrouded in unbearable humidity—hike to La Coca Waterfall, take in the green canopy from Yokahú Tower, and keep an ear out for singing coquí frogs.

Where to stay: For luxe accommodations just a 25-minute drive from El Yunque, look no further than Four Seasons Resort and Residences Puerto Rico, which coordinates guided treks with a strong emphasis on Indigenous history. Condado Ocean Club offers direct access to the beach, while this lakefront retreat near Cueva Ventana and Arecibo Observatory is ideal for couples seeking verdant views.

When to go: December–MarchAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Another destination where US travelers can leave their passports at home, the US Virgin Islands are a quintessential Caribbean paradise. December through March is peak season, and there are plenty of reasons why—no rain, calm seas, and temperatures that hover between 77 and 85 degrees, to name a few. St. Croix, the largest of the USVI’s three main islands, is defined by the white sands of Rainbow Beach, as well as its Danish ancestry, which you can explore at colonial-era sites like Fort Frederik and Fort Christiansvaern. St. John is filled with all kinds of natural wonders; take the Underwater Snorkel Trail at Trunk Bay to peer at parrotfish, or set off on the three-mile Reef Bay Trail to hike among pre-Columbian petroglyphs painted by Taíno Indians. St. Thomas is a bustling port with cosmopolitan charm, and you’d be well advised to sample a few conch fritters at Gladys' Café. Whichever island you choose, clear skies and turquoise waters await.

Where to stay: One of Traveler’s favorite private island resorts (and the only one in the US Virgin Islands), Lovango Resort and Beach Club is located across St. John’s Caneel Bay and offers all kinds of eco-chic accommodations, from wooden treehouses to explorer-style tents. The Westin St. Thomas is set right in front of the harbor, with a stellar spa worth traveling for. For something a bit more intimate, this light-filled, two-bedroom cottage is just a five-minute walk away from Cruz Beach.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 65 degrees

While temperatures do drop in Marrakech during the winter—the peaks of the Atlas Mountains will be blanketed in snow—you’ll see far more sun than in certain parts of the US; plus, it’s all the more reason to enjoy a steamy hammam. Winter is a great time to explore the city's popular sites with thinner crowds: comb through the medina’s bustling souks for fragrant spices and a pair of babouche slippers, take in the cobalt blue buildings at the Jardin Majorelle, or learn about one of France’s most legendary fashion designers at the Yves Saint Laurent Museum. Keep an eye out for the dates of the Marrakech International Film Festival, which takes place between the months of November and December—this year it falls from November 20 to 28, and features 76 films from 39 countries.

Where to stay: Traveler contributor Jordan Lippe-McGraw is a big fan of this family-friendly villa, with a heated pool, hammam, and cinema room. A Triple Crown winner, La Mamounia is the city’s grand dame. As global features director Erin Florio puts it, “Every inch of this palatial property has been hyper-considered to make the guest feel as though they have arrived in some regal estate of an Arabian kingdom.” At the Royal Mansour, all riads come with 24/7 access to a private butler.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–90 degrees

The Arenal Volcano looms over Costa Rica’s La Fortuna region, heating its natural springs, and there’s a greater chance you’ll see it without cloud cover in the winter. For travelers seeking a combo of adventure and relaxation, La Fortuna (about a three-hour drive from San José) is well-suited for both. Hike through cooled lava fields at Arenal Volcano National Park or swim around La Fortuna Waterfall, then take advantage of nature’s healing powers at Tabacón Thermal Resort and Spa. For a truly memorable experience, book a tour with Arenal Horse Tours and ride your steed straight into the Arenal River for a refreshing dip.

Where to stay: While Tabacón is perhaps the most iconic resort in the area, The Springs Resort & Spa is another great option, boasting two dozen hot springs, pools, and waterfalls spread across the 65-acre property. If you’re looking for something more intimate, this forest cabin features a private spring-fed pool, rain shower, and marked hiking trails—a one-of-a-kind off-grid retreat.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80–85 degrees

Though small, this Central American country offers a diversity of experiences, whether you want to take it slow in a charming fishing village or ascend new heights in the jungle. Perhaps the most popular destination on Belize’s tourism map, Ambergris Caye is a departure point for the country’s barrier reef—though just south of Ambergris Caye, Caye Caulker provides a nice alternative. While on the car-free island, book a tour with Ragga Sail Adventures for a half-day snorkel through Hol Chan Marine Reserve, the oldest marine reserve in the country. Further south in Punta Gorda, you’ll find rugged adventures and a strong sense of Mayan culture. Here, you’ll have access to several offshore cayes (Belize has hundreds of these small islands, brimming with marine life), from Snake Cayes to Sapodilla Cayes Marine Reserve; if you prefer jungle, take a boat tour through the Monkey River, or hike to the waterfall at Rio Blanco National Park. And be sure to explore the surrounding Toledo District for Mayan ruins, like the Lubaantun, which dates back to 700–900 AD and is also an excellent site for birdwatching.

Where to stay: Nestled within the Belizean rainforest, Copal Tree Lodge’s jungle suites will make you feel as though you’re suspended among the trees. Wake up to the sounds of monkeys every morning, then take a farm tour around the surrounding property, where you’ll discover how cacao, vanilla, and sugar cane grow. Over in San Pedro, Alaia Belize is your luxury option, just 600 yards away from the barrier reef, while this tiny home will make you feel as though you’re vacationing in a fairy tale.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 80 degrees

December through April is peak vacation time in Punta Cana, when the rainy season has subsided and there’s not a cloud in the sky. With average highs in the 80s and average lows in the 70s, you’re likely to experience perfect weather during your stay. Come February, you’ve got a good chance of spotting some humpback whales if you cast your eyes off the coast of the Península de Samaná, where they typically pass through until April. The country also celebrates Independence Day in February—on the 27th, to be exact. Visit around that time, and you’re bound to run into a Carnaval parade or bachata dance circle. With the Cordillera Oriental mountain range looming in the background and a selection of cenotes around town—from Hoyo Azul to Hoyo Claro—mountain buggy excursions and diving adventures await even in the winter.

Where to stay: The W Punta Cana redefines the all-inclusive resort as we know it with top-tier dining and some of the largest rooms in the country. Hyatt Vivid Punta Cana, which just opened its doors in August 2026, is another upscale all-inclusive in the area, boasting swim-out suites and a chic speakeasy. If you’ve got kids in tow but still want to experience the height of luxury, Eden Roc Cap Cana is a consistent Readers' Choice Awards winner. For a villa the whole family will enjoy, this eight-bedroom Airbnb in Tortuga Bay comes with a private pool.

When to go: December–AprilAverage winter temperature: 70 degrees

Another prime location for whale watching, Baja California’s southern tip sees the migration of humpback and gray whales between the months of December and April (you might even elect to swim with whale sharks, too, which roam around the nearby Bay of La Paz around this time). You’ll have just missed the rainy season in November, making way for sunny, 70-degree beach days and not-too-chilly evenings. The creative town of Todos Santos boasts a number of art galleries to pop into, like Galeria de Todos Santos and La Sonrisa de la Muerte, while the Sierra de la Laguna mountains are home to stunning trails and swimming holes. If you’re a surfer, Playa Los Cerritos and Playa San Pedro offer some of Mexico’s best waves.

Where to stay: Todos Santos is home to a number of cutting-edge boutique hotels. Hotel San Cristobal, with its vibrant interiors and delectably fresh seafood, perfectly embodies the bohemian vibes of this tiny surf town. Paradero Todos Santos, located on a five-and-a-half-acre farm, is designed around outdoor adventure: Pick the “Unbound” option, and surfing, hiking, and biking experiences will all be included in the nightly fare. If you prefer to go the rental route, this little bungalow is set among farmland in Pescadero, with its own private rooftop.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 75 degrees

Miami is a good idea any time of year, but December through February is considered the dry season, promising temperatures in the mid-70s. Two important events pop up this time of year: Art Basel Miami, in December (4–6, this year), and the South Beach Wine & Food Festival, in February (running the 25–28 in 2027). But there’s always something to do in the Magic City, whether that’s taking a peek into the Pérez Art Museum, spending money in the Design District, or having a stroll through the Fairchild Tropical Botanic Garden.

Where to stay: To embrace the happy-go-lucky spirit of the locals, check in to the Goodtime Hotel and sip on a Purple Reign cocktail (co-owner Pharrell’s favorite drink) at the rooftop pool club. If you’d like to tap into the city’s Art Deco architectural history, stay at The Moore, where you’ll be close to Wynwood and Downtown Miami. This dreamy loft in Collins Park, just a short walk to the beach, is a good bet too.

When to go: December–FebruaryAverage winter temperature: 85 degrees

Depending on where you’re coming from, Cape Town might be a little out of the way. But the US's winter is their summer, and with that comes sunny days and a dry, Mediterranean-like climate. Around mid-January, tourists start to flee and kids return to school, making popular attractions more accessible. Take a cable car (or hike, if you’re feeling bold) up to the famous Table Mountain, or drive to Boulders Beach, which boasts one of the last colonies of African penguins in the world. There are plenty of opportunities to engage with some art, as well, from the contemporary galleries at Zeitz MOCAA to the rainbow houses of the Bo-Kaap Museum. And if you’re feeling especially adventurous, you can treat Cape Town as a jumping-off point for the famed Garden Route road trip.
